en: The Dharma taught in each Veda is the first [source of Dharma]. We shall now explain its [further] exposition. The second is that which is based on the Smṛtis. The third is the tradition of the Śiṣṭas. The Śiṣṭas are indeed those who are free from envy, devoid of egoism, possessing only as much grain as fits in a jar, lacking greed, and being exempt from hypocrisy, pride, avarice, delusion, and anger.

Those for whom the Veda, along with its supplements, has been acquired through the Dharma, are the cultured (śiṣṭas); they are knowers who infer that [the Dharma], and their authority is based on both revelation and perception. //6//
In their absence, an assembly of at least ten persons [constitutes a court]. Moreover, they quote this:

"One learned in the four Vedas, one capable of interpreting them, one who knows the auxiliary sciences (aṅgas), one who recites the Dharma, and three Brahmins established in their respective stages of life (āśramas)—this is an assembly of at least ten."
There may be five, or three, or even one who is irreproachable;
for one who can speak according to the Dharma, there are not thousands of others.
Just as an elephant made of wood, just as a deer made of leather, so too is a Brahmin who has not studied; these three are bearers of names only. ||10||
Whatever those fools, deluded by darkness and ignorant of the Dharma, say—that sin becomes a hundredfold and falls upon the speakers themselves. (11)
The path of the Dharma, which has many doors, is subtle and difficult to follow;
therefore, when there is doubt, it should not be explained by a single person, even if he is highly learned.
The twice-born, mounted upon the chariot of the Dharmaśāstras and wielding the sword of the Vedas, whatever they may say even in jest, that is remembered as the supreme Dharma. (13)
Just as water situated within a stone may be destroyed by wind and sun,
so too whatever sin exists in the doer dissolves completely like water.
Having carefully considered the body, strength, lifespan, age, time, and the nature of the act, one who knows the Dharma should prescribe the penances with his intellect. (15)
"For those who lack vows, who lack mantras, and who subsist merely by birth—even if they have gathered in their thousands—the status of an assembly does not exist. (16)
Thus ends the first section of the first book in the Dharma-sūtra of Baudhāyana.

There are five types of misconduct: to the south and likewise to the north. (1) We shall explain those that occur to the south. (2) Namely: eating with one who has not been initiated; eating with a woman; eating food that has been kept overnight; and sexual intercourse with the daughters of one's maternal uncle or paternal aunt. (3)
Now, to the north: the sale of wool, the drinking of *sīdhu* liquor, trade with people from both sides of the sea, the profession of arms, and seafaring. 4.
Performing one thing in place of another, one becomes culpable for performing the other in place of the first. In each such case, the authority of local custom alone would prevail.
"This is false," says Gautama; for one should not respect either [of these views], since they are seen to contradict the tradition of the learned (śiṣṭa-smṛti).
"Some say it is the space between the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā. Now, moreover, the Bhāllavins cite this verse regarding this matter:
"Behind lies the Sindhu, the supporter, and ahead is the rising of the sun;
as long as the Kṛṣṇas run, so long indeed shall there be spiritual luster. ||12||
The Avantyas, the Aṅgas and Magadhas, the Surāṣṭras, the people of the South, the Upāvṛts, and the Sindhu-Sauvīras—these are of mixed origin. ||13||
Having gone to the Āraṭṭas, Kāraskaras, Puṇḍras, Sauvīras, Vaṅgas, Kaliṅgas, and Prānūnas, one should perform the Punastoma sacrifice, or rather, the Sarvapṛṣṭhā. Furthermore, they cite this:
"He who enters the Kaliṅgas commits a sin with his feet;
the seers have declared that the expiation for him is the Vaiśvānara oblation."
Regarding the determination of guilt for even many offenses committed, they praise the Pavitreṣṭi sacrifice, for it is the supreme means of purification. ||16||
Moreover, they cite this:
"By performing the Vaiśvānarī, the Vrātapatī, and likewise the Pavitreṣṭi sacrifice at each seasonal juncture, one is liberated from sins."
"One is completely liberated from evils. ||17||
Thus ends the second section in the first book of the Dharma-sūtra of Baudhāyana.
Thus ends the first chapter of the first book in the Dharma-sūtra of Baudhāyana.

The ancient Vedic studentship lasts forty-eight years. (1) Or twenty-four, or twelve, for each Veda. (2) Or at least one year for each *kāṇḍa*. (3) Or until [the Veda] has been mastered, because life is unstable. (4) "One should establish the sacred fires while his hair is still black," so says the Śruti. (5)
"Until the binding of the girdle of munja grass, they do not restrict his ritual actions;
for he is equal to a Śūdra in his mode of livelihood until he is born through the Veda. (6)

The number of years begins from conception; among those, he should initiate a Brāhmaṇa in the eighth [year], a Rājanya in the eleventh [year] (three more), and a Vaiśya in the twelfth [year] (one more than that).

Spring, summer, and autumn are the seasons in their sequential order. [These are associated] with the *gāyatrī*, *triṣṭubh*, and *jagatī* meters respectively. Their time limits, without transgression, are up to sixteen, twenty-two, and twenty-four years respectively.

The girdles are made of muñja grass, a bowstring, or hemp. (13) The skins are those of the black antelope, the spotted deer, and the goat. (14) The staffs, made from a tree suitable for sacrifice, are measured by the height of the head, the forehead, or the tip of the nose. (15)

One should go for alms with the word "bhavat" at the beginning, "bhavat" in the middle, and ending with "yācñā," [uttering] the seven syllables "kṣāṃ hiṃ" without adding anything further. (16) A Brāhmaṇa should beg with "bhavat" at the beginning, a Rājanya with "bhavat" in the middle, and a Vaiśya with "bhavat" at the end, among all the social classes. (17) These [classes], beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, remain established in their own respective duties. (18)

Having fetched sacrificial fuel from the forest, he should place it on the fire (19). He should be truthful in speech, modest, and free from pride (20). Rising before [others] and retiring to bed after them (21), he should never disregard the word of his teacher, except in the case of a mortal sin (22). He should converse with women only as much as is necessary (23). He should avoid dancing, singing, instrumental music, perfumes, garlands, wearing shoes or carrying an umbrella, and the use of collyrium and ointments (24).

He should grasp the teacher’s right foot with his right hand and the left foot with his left hand. (25) If he desires long life and heaven, he may do so at will for another person of virtuous conduct, provided he has been authorized by his teacher. (26) He should touch [the teacher’s] ears while saying, “I am so-and-so, sir,” for the purpose of concentrating the mind. (27) [He should grasp the feet] below the knees down to the feet. (28)

One should not [greet] while seated [another] who is not seated; nor while lying down [another] who is not lying down; nor when one is unpurified [another] who is unpurified. (29) Within one's capacity, one should not remain unpurified for even a moment. (30) One should not offer salutation with firewood, a water-pot, flowers, or food in hand, nor with anything else that is similarly occupied. (31) One should not offer salutation in a crowded assembly, except in extreme cases. (32) One who has attained virility may [offer salutation] to the wives of brothers and to the young wives of gurus. (33) There is no fault in sitting together on a boat, a stone, a wooden plank, an elephant, a palace, a mat, or on revolving vehicles. (34)

Adorning, massaging, bathing, and eating the leftovers [of food] belong to the teacher (guru). (35) These, with the exception of eating the leftovers, belong to his son or to one who has studied the Vedas (anūcāna). (36) And these, with the exception of adorning, massaging, bathing, and eating the leftovers, belong to his wife. (37)
One should run after him as he runs, follow him as he goes, and stand by him as he stands. ||38||
One who is proud should not bathe in water; he should float like a staff.

In times of distress, one may study under a non-Brāhmaṇa; [41] as well as perform service and follow him for as long as the study lasts. [42] For those two, that very [service] is the means of purification. [43] The same applies toward brothers, sons, and pupils. [44] However, one must rise to greet and address younger officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), fathers-in-law, paternal uncles, and maternal uncles. [45] Kātya maintains that this refers to the formal return-greeting (*pratyabhivāda*). [46] This is because it is observed in the case of the child Āṅgirasa. [47]
Thus ends the third section in the first book of the *Dharmasūtra* of Baudhāyana.
Where neither dharma nor wealth is found, nor even a corresponding desire to serve,
one should rather die with one's learning than sow it upon barren soil.
Like fire consuming dry grass, sacred knowledge burns one who disregards its source;
therefore, one should never speak of sacred knowledge to those who treat it with contempt. (2)
Thus they make this speech known to him. ||3||

Brahman indeed delivered the creatures to Death; he did not deliver the religious student (*brahmacārin*) to him. He said, "Let there be for me also a share in this," [to which it was replied], "On whatever night one does not bring sacrificial fuel. ||4||

Therefore, for whatever night a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*) does not bring firewood, he dwells having cut away a portion of his own life-span. Therefore, a student of sacred knowledge should bring firewood, thinking: "Lest I dwell having cut away a portion of my life-span. ||5||

He who enters upon the student life (brahmacarya) enters upon a long sacrificial session (sattra). The fuel-stick he places when entering is the introductory offering (prāyaṇīyā); that which he places when about to bathe is the concluding offering (udayanīyā); and those which he places in between are his sacrificial sessions.

When a Brāhmaṇa enters upon the life of a student (*brahmacarya*), he enters the beings fourfold: one foot in Agni, one foot in Death, one foot in the Teacher, and his fourth foot remains in himself. When he places fuel on the fire, he ransoms that foot of his which is in Agni; having consecrated it, he places it in himself, and it enters him. Then, when he makes himself poor, becomes shameless, begs for alms, and practices the life of a student, he ransoms that foot of his which is in Death; having consecrated it, he places it in himself, and it enters him. Then, when he obeys the word of the teacher, he ransoms that foot of his which is in the teacher; having consecrated it, he places it in himself, and it enters him. Then, when he studies his private recitation (*svādhyāya*), he ransoms that foot of his which is in himself; having consecrated it, he places it in himself, and it enters him. He should certainly not beg for alms after he has performed the ceremonial bath (*snāna*). Even though he has performed the bath, he may still go begging for alms, even from his relatives, even from his ancestors, and for other ritual purposes. If he cannot find anyone else from whom to beg, he may beg even from his own teacher’s wife, or even from his own mother. He should not let seven nights pass without having begged.
There is a fault in failing to practice begging for alms and in failing to kindle the sacred fire;
if one fails to do this for seven nights, one should perform the penance of an *avakīrṇin*.

All the Vedas enter him who knows this and lives in this manner. Just as a fire, when well-kindled, shines forth, even so does he shine after his bath who, knowing this, practices the life of a student—so says the Brāhmaṇa. Thus ends the Brāhmaṇa.
Thus ends the fourth section in the first book of the Dharma Sūtra of Baudhāyana.
Thus ends the second chapter in the first book of the Dharma-sūtra of Baudhāyana.

Now, concerning the *snātaka*: 1. He shall have an inner garment and an upper garment. 2. He shall carry a bamboo staff. 3. And a water-pot containing water. 4. He shall wear two sacred threads (*yajñopavīta*). 5. [He shall also possess] a turban, a deerskin as an upper garment, sandals, an umbrella, the *aupāsana* fire, and the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices. 6. On the festival days (*parvan*), he shall have his hair, beard, body hair, and nails shaved. 7.

His mode of life is as follows: [8] He should seek raw food among Brāhmaṇas, Rājanyas, Vaiśyas, and Rathakāras; [9] or he may seek alms. [10] He should remain silent while standing. [11] And he should perform all his *bhūti*-rites associated with the gods and ancestors belonging to the category of *pākayajña* sacrifices. [12] According to Baudhāyana, by this rule the great seers of Prajāpati Parameṣṭhin attained the highest goal. [13]
Thus ends the fifth section in the first book of the Dharma-sūtra of Baudhāyana.
Thus ends the third chapter of the first book in the Dharma-sūtra of Baudhāyana.
Now they teach the practice of the water-pot. ||1||
Fire is declared to reside in the right ear of a goat, in the right hand of a Brahmin, in water, and in a clump of Kuśa grass.

Therefore, having performed the purification, one should wipe it with the hand; for that constitutes the rite of circumambulation by fire. By reciting "Shine forth, O Jātavedas," it is distinguished from a mere re-burning. ||2||

In that case as well, if one should perceive anything touched by *kuśa* grass or by blades of grass, one should kindle a fire and perform a circumambulation while burning it clockwise. From this point forward, they teach that for those [fires] defiled by dogs, crows, and the like, the color of the fire itself is the indicator [of purity]. For those defiled by urine, feces, blood, semen, and so forth, there must be a complete abandonment [of the fire].
If the water-pot is broken, one should offer a hundred oblations with the Vyāhṛtis or recite them.
"Earth has gone to Earth; mother has gone to mother.
May we abound with sons and cattle; may he who hates us be split asunder."

Having gathered the skull-bowls and cast them into the waters, and having performed the Sāvitrī rite at least ten times, he should take up another [vessel] again. Taking refuge in Varuṇa, [he should recite]: "This, O Varuṇa, is for thee; mayest thou [grant] me once more, Om. He should meditate upon the syllable.
Having received [the fee] from a Śūdra, one should perform a hundred [times]; from a Vaiśya, fifty is prescribed;
from a Kṣatriya, twenty-five; and from a Brāhmaṇa, ten are proclaimed.

"When the sun has set, should one take water or not? thus do the exponents of Brahman deliberate. "One should take it"—this is another view. As much water as one takes, for so long should one restrain the breath. For fire indeed takes up the water.

As long as his hands and feet remain wet after being sprinkled with water from a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu), he is impure to others; however, he purifies himself alone. It is understood that he should perform no other ritual action [during that time]. Or rather, according to Baudhāyana, he is pure up to the wrists for each act of purification.
Moreover, they also cite this: ||16||
Thus ends the sixth section in the first book of the Baudhāyana Dharmasūtra.
The water-pot was ordained of old by Brahmā and the foremost of sages for the sake of the purification of the twice-born; therefore, one should always carry it.
Therefore, purification, drinking, and the twilight worship must be performed without hesitation by one who desires his own welfare. (1)
The wise person should act with a pure mind and should not defile their consciousness;
since the Self-existent One was born together with the water-pot (kamaṇḍalu), one should therefore move about with a water-pot. ||2||

While performing the evacuation of urine or feces, one takes [the soil] with the right hand, while the left hand is used for the ritual rinsing (ācamana); this is established as the practice of the virtuous. ||3||
Just as a cup is called pure through its contact with Soma, so too the water-pot is eternally pure through its contact with water. (4)
Therefore, one should avoid him during the rites for the ancestors, the gods, and the sacred fires. ||5||

Therefore, one should not travel on a road without a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu), nor to the end of a boundary, nor from house to house. Some say one should not even go a single step further than the distance of an arrow's length. Baudhāyana says that if one desires the continuity of dharma, [one should carry it]. "By means of the Ṛgveda," so speaks Vāc; "by means of the Ṛgveda," so speaks Vāc.
Thus ends the seventh section in the first book of the Dharma-sūtra of Baudhāyana.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the first book of the Dharma-sūtra of Baudhāyana.
Now, therefore, follows the foundation of purification. 1.
The limbs are purified by water; the intellect is purified by knowledge;
the elemental self is purified by non-violence; and the mind is purified by truth. ||2||
Purity of mind is internal purity. (3) We shall now explain external purity. (4)

The sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*) is made of *kauśa* grass or of thread, and it consists of three strands twisted three times each. (5) It reaches down to the navel. (6) Having raised the right arm and placed the left under it, one should place it over the head. (7) For the ancestors, it is the reverse. (8) When it is suspended around the neck, it is the *nivīta* position. (9) When it is suspended below [the arms], it is the *adhovīta* position. (10)

Seated facing either the east or the north, one should begin the rite of purification in a clean place, having placed the right arm between the knees and having washed both feet and hands up to the wrists. (11) One should not sip water using the residue from the washing of the feet. (12) If one should sip water, one must first pour that residue onto the ground and then sip water. (13)

One should sip water using the *brāhma* tīrtha. (14) The base of the thumb is the *brāhma* tīrtha; (15) the tip of the thumb is the *pitrya*; the tips of the fingers are the *daiva*; and the base of the fingers is the *ārṣa*. (16)

[He should not sip water] with his fingers, nor with those having bubbles, nor with those having foam, nor with warm [water], nor with alkaline, nor with salty, nor with turbid, nor with discolored [water], nor with foul-smelling or foul-tasting [water]. (17) Neither laughing, nor talking, nor standing, nor looking around, nor bent over, nor prostrate, nor with his hair-locks untied, nor with his neck covered, nor with his head wrapped, nor in haste, nor without the sacred thread, nor with feet outstretched, nor with his girdle tied, nor with knees apart, nor making any sound. (18) He should drink water reaching the heart three times. (19) He should wipe [his mouth] three times. (20) Some say twice. (21) For a Śūdra and for a woman, both [acts] are done once. (22) Moreover, they quote this:

A Brahmin becomes pure by water that has reached his heart; a pure Kṣatriya, by water reaching his throat; a Vaiśya, by water that has been sipped; and a woman or a Śūdra, by merely touching it at the end. ||23||

When food adheres to the teeth, it is like the teeth themselves; because they are held there like the teeth, one need not rinse when such particles have fallen away, for their purity is like that of the saliva flowing from them. ||24||
Moreover, they also cite this:
"Regarding food stuck between the teeth, as well as what may be inside the mouth, and what remains after sipping water (ācamana)—one becomes pure by simply swallowing it. (25)
Having touched the cavities with water, one should touch the feet, the navel, the head, and finally the left hand. ||26||

If he becomes impure by taking up something made of metal, he should discard it, sip water, and, before taking it up again, sprinkle it with water. (27) Now, if he becomes impure by [taking] food, he should discard it, sip water, and, before taking it up again, sprinkle it with water. (28) Now, if he becomes impure by [taking] water, he should discard it, sip water, and, before taking it up again, sprinkle it with water. (29) This same procedure is reversed in the case of a vessel. (30) In the case of an object made of wood, there is an option. (31)

The purification of metallic vessels that have been defiled by food remnants is performed by scrubbing them with cow dung, earth, or ashes, or with any one of these. (32) Copper, silver, and gold are purified with acidic liquids. (33) Earthenware vessels are purified by burning. (34) Wooden vessels are purified by planing. (35) Vessels made of bamboo are purified with cow dung. (36) Vessels made of fruit are purified with a rope of cow hair. (37) Black antelope skins are purified with *bilva* rice-grains. (38) Woolen blankets (*kutapa*) are purified with *ariṣṭa* fruits. (39) Blankets made of sheep’s wool are purified by exposure to the sun. (40) Linen cloth is purified with a paste of white mustard seeds. (41) Cotton cloth is purified with earth. (42) Leather is purified in the same manner as cloth. (43) Stones and gems are purified in the same manner as metallic vessels. (44) Bone is purified in the same manner as wood. (45) Conch-shells, horns, mother-of-pearl, and ivory are purified in the same manner as linen cloth, or with milk. (46–47)

Or, for those items mentioned previously that have been touched by urine, feces, blood, semen, or a corpse, one should wipe them twenty-one times with something agreeable to the eyes and nose. Such non-metallic objects should be discarded in this manner.
On account of the scriptural injunction regarding the cup-vessels at the sacrifice, there is the Vedic revelation: "They do not become defiled by Soma. (Sūtras 50–51)
Time, fire, purity of mind, smearing with water and the like, and the unawareness of living beings—this is said to be the sixfold purification. ||52||
Moreover, they cite this:
"Having understood the time, the place, as well as oneself, the substance, the purpose of the substance, the occasion, and the circumstances, one who knows purification should perform purification."
One who is skilled and desirous of wholesome qualities should practice accordingly. ||53||
Thus ends the eighth section in the first book of the Dharma-sūtra of Baudhāyana.
The hand of an artisan is always pure, as is merchandise that has been displayed for sale;
almsfood received by a student of sacred knowledge is always pure—so says the Vedic revelation.
A calf is pure when discharging its milk; a bird is pure when plucking fruit;
women are pure during sexual union; and a dog is pure when seizing game.
All mines are pure, with the exception of the mine of liquor;
likewise, continuous streams are undefiled, as are particles of dust raised by the wind. (3)
And as for those trees planted in impure places that bear flowers and fruit—even their flowers and fruits are not considered defiled. (4)
Having touched a sacred tree, a funeral pyre, a sacrificial post, a Caṇḍāla, or a seller of the Vedas,
a Brāhmaṇa shall enter the water with his clothes on.
One’s own bed, seat, clothing, wife, children, and water-pot—these are pure for oneself, but impure for others. (6)
A seat, a bed, a vehicle, boats, and grass on the road—
these are purified by the wind alone even when touched by a Caṇḍāla or an outcast.

Whatever grain is found in threshing floors, whatever water is in wells and ponds, and whatever milk is found in a cow-pen—even from those sources that are otherwise unfit for consumption, it is fit to be used. (8)
The gods ordained three purifiers for the Brāhmaṇas:
that which is unseen, that which is washed with water, and that which is commended by speech. (9)
Water that has reached the ground is pure when it is sufficient to satisfy a cow's thirst, provided it is not contaminated by impurities and possesses its natural fragrance, color, and taste. (10)

The purification of the ground is achieved through sweeping, sprinkling, smearing, spreading [grass], and scraping, according to the specific defect and the appropriate location. Furthermore, they cite this example:
Thus ends the ninth section in the first book of the Dharma-sūtra of Baudhāyana.
A drop of water the size of a cow’s hide, when poured upon the ground, purifies it—whether it was previously covered with impurity or not—provided that no trace of the impurity is perceived. ||1||
When food has been placed on the fire out of sight, one should take a portion and sprinkle it with water; likewise for foods that are to be sold in the market.
For the gods are loathsome and desire purity; they do not accept the oblation of one who lacks faith. ||4||
Moreover, they cite this example:
"Having examined both the impure person who lacks faith and the pure person who possesses faith, the gods ordained that their food be equal."
But Prajāpati said to them: "That is not equal; for it is unequal.
That which is offered by one lacking faith is destroyed, whereas that which is purified by faith is superior. (5)
Moreover, they cite this:
"Lack of faith is the supreme evil; faith indeed is the supreme austerity.
Therefore, the deities do not consume an oblation given without faith. (6)
Even after sacrificing or giving gifts, a fool does not go to heaven.
One whose conduct is destroyed by doubt, who relies on his own personal opinions, and who transgresses the scriptures is considered a fool because he obstructs the continuity of the Dharma. (8)
But for vegetables, flowers, fruits, roots, and medicinal herbs, there shall be washing. ||9||
Having set aside dry grass, wood unfit for sacrifice, or a clod of earth, one should urinate or defecate during the day and night facing north or south, with the head covered.

In the case of urine, there is cleansing with earth and water [once]. (11) For the hand, it is three times. (12) The same applies to feces. (13) For the anus and the hands, there are three applications each in succession. (14) Upon the emission of semen, it is as in the case of urine. (15)

Having loosened the knot of his lower garment and put it on again, he should touch water; (16) or he should touch moist grass, cow dung, or the earth. (17) One engaged in ritual action should avoid touching anything below the navel. (18) For the Śruti declares: "Above the navel of a man is pure, but what is below is impure. (19)
For Śūdras who are supervised by Āryans, there shall be shaving every half-month or every month, and the procedure for sipping water (ācamana) shall be as for an Āryan.
A Vaiśya may subsist by money-lending; it should be at the rate of five māṣas for every twenty [units of currency].
Moreover, they cite this example: "He who, having taken a loan at a low price, causes it to be repaid at a high price—
he is indeed called a usurer, and is censured in all religious laws."
He weighed the killing of an embryo against usury on a scale;
the killer of the embryo remained steady at the end, while the usurer trembled. (23)
One should treat cowherds, merchants, artisans, actors and musicians, servants, usurers, and even Brahmins [who act improperly] as one would Śūdras. (24)
However, one may give the two former [gifts] to a most wicked person who is greedy, an atheist, and whose sense of duty has been utterly destroyed. ||25||
Families fall into a state of non-nobility through the absence of sacrifice, the absence of marriage, the neglect of the Veda, and by the slighting of Brahmins. (26)
There is no transgression against a Brahmin who is foolish and devoid of sacred knowledge;
for one does not offer oblations into ashes after setting aside a blazing fire.
Families that are deficient in sacred counsel fall from their noble status—even those possessing cattle, horses, vehicles, and the fruits of agriculture or royal service. (28)
But those families that are enriched by mantras, even if they possess little wealth, are reckoned among the noble lineages and acquire great renown. (29)
Vedic study leads to the ruin of agriculture, and agriculture leads to the ruin of Vedic study.
One who is capable may practice both; however, one who is incapable should abandon agriculture. (30)
Truly, the gods do not partake [of offerings] from one who is corpulent, lacks self-restraint, bellows loudly like a bull,
has a dangling belly, is impetuous, and speaks according to his own whims.
There, those who are emaciated go as minute beings. ||31||
Whatever one acts with heedlessness in youth—
whether good or bad, of whatever kind or at whatever time—
if one conducts oneself virtuously in later life, [that former conduct is cast aside].
That alone belongs to him, and not the others. ||32||
One should constantly grieve in one's mind, reflecting upon one's evil deeds;
then, being ascetic and vigilant, one is liberated from that sin.
Drops that touch the feet of one who is rinsing the mouth for others do not cause the state of being "impure with remnants" (ucchiṣṭa); they are equal to those drops that fall upon the ground. (34)
Thus ends the tenth section in the first book of the Baudhāyana Dharmasūtra.

Regarding birth and death, they declare that the period of impurity for sapindas lasts ten days, with the exception of officiating priests, those initiated for sacrifice, and religious students (brahmacārins). (1) Sapinda-relationship, however, extends to the seventh degree among sapindas. (2) Until seven months have passed, or until the eruption of teeth, there is merely the touching of water (for purification). (3)
The rites of offering rice-balls and water for one deceased who has not reached three years of age are not prescribed; nor should cremation be performed until the eruption of teeth. (4)
And [he should offer] when the maidens have not yet been given away; some, however, do so when they have been given away. ||5-6||
For women are considered to be without mantras for the sake of winning over the world.
For female relatives who have not yet been married, the kinsmen become pure after three days;
and those of the same lineage (sanābhayaḥ) become pure according to the very rule already stated. ||8||

Moreover, the great-grandfather, the grandfather, the father, one's own uterine brothers, the son of a woman of the same caste, the son, the grandson, and the great-grandson—excluding the sons of these latter—and their sons and grandsons, as long as the inheritance has not been divided, are called *sapiṇḍas*. Those whose inheritance has been divided are also called *sakulyas*.

For when others are absent, the property goes to him [the deceased]. (11) In the absence of sapindas, a sakulya [takes it]. (12) In his absence, the father, teacher, pupil, or officiating priest shall take it. (13) In their absence, the king shall bestow that property upon those who are learned in the three Vedas and are advanced in years. (14) But the king must never himself take the property of a Brahmin. (15) Moreover, they cite this: "The property of a Brahmin destroys one's sons and grandsons; it carries off the solitary man like poison. They say that 'poison' is not truly poison; the property of a Brahmin is called poison. (16)
Therefore, a king should not take the property of a Brāhmaṇa; for the property of a Brāhmaṇa is indeed the most potent poison. ||16||

In the case of a coincidence of birth and death, the period of impurity is the same, lasting ten nights. (17) Now, if several periods of ten nights should coincide, the impurity lasts for the first ten-night period, up to the ninth day. (18) Regarding birth, the impurity for the mother and father lasts ten days. (19) Some say it belongs to the mother alone, because she carries the child. (20) Others say it belongs to the father, because of the predominance of the seed. (21) For indeed, sons are heard of in scripture as being born without a womb. (22) But [the impurity] belongs to both the mother and father, because of the commonality of their physical contact. (23)

But at death, having placed the child first, having arranged the sacred threads over the right shoulder (apasavya), having descended to a bathing place and immersed themselves three times each, having emerged and sipped water, having poured out water with the intention directed toward him, and having emerged from there and sipped water again, they shall touch charcoal and water at the door of the house; then, eating food that is neither pungent nor salty, they shall sit upon mats for ten days.
The Śrāddha rite should be performed on either the eleventh or the twelfth day. Regarding the remaining rites, one should conform to worldly custom.

In this case as well, among those who are not *sapiṇḍa* relatives, one should observe impurity for three nights, one day and night, or one day, according to their proximity. (27) For the teacher (*ācārya*), the sub-teacher (*upādhyāya*), and their sons, it is three nights. (28) And so too for officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). (29) For students (*śiṣya*), fellow students (*satīrthya*), and co-students (*sabrahmacārin*), one should observe impurity for three nights, one day and night, or one day. (30)
In the case of a miscarriage, for women, the nights [of impurity] are equal in number to the months of gestation. ||31||
If one touches a corpse unintentionally, one becomes pure immediately after touching water while clothed; if intentionally, it is for three nights.
And [the same applies] when she has reached her season. 34. He who is born from that [union] is called "accursed" (abhiśasta); her religious observances have been explained. 35.
Having touched one who sells the Vedas, a sacrificial post, a fallen funeral pyre,
a dog, or an outcaste, one should perform a bath.
If a worm should arise from the wound of a Brahmin where pus and blood have formed, what would be the expiation for that? (37)
Cow’s urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water infused with *kuśa* grass—
one who has been bitten by a worm shall become pure by bathing and drinking these for three days.

One who has been bitten by a dog should plunge into water while still wearing his clothes. Or, having washed that spot and touched it with fire, and having washed [himself] again and sipped water for the feet, he becomes pure. Furthermore, they cite this:
"A Brahmin who has been bitten by a dog goes to a river that flows into the ocean, performs a hundred breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*), and becomes purified by consuming clarified butter."
"Having bathed with gold and silver, or with water from the horns of cows, or with nine new jars, one becomes pure immediately. ||41||
Thus ends the eleventh section in the first book of the Dharmasūtra of Baudhāyana.
Domestic animals are not to be eaten. (1) Nor are carnivorous birds. (2) Likewise, the cock and the pig. (3) With the exception of the goat and the sheep. (4)

The porcupine, the monitor lizard, the hare, the porcupine-fish, the tortoise, and the rhinoceros—these five five-toed animals are edible, with the exception of the rhinoceros. (5) Likewise, the ruru deer, the common deer, the spotted deer, the buffalo, and the boar—these five two-hoofed animals are edible, with the exception of the kuluṅga deer. (6)

Among birds, the partridge, the pigeon, the francolin, the vārdhrāṇasa, and the peacock—excluding the vāraṇa—are the five "scattered-feeders" (viṣkira). Among fish, the sahasradaṃṣṭra, the cilicima, the varmi, the bṛhacchiras, the śakula, the rohita, and the rājīva [are permitted].

The milk of a cow in the first ten days after calving is unfit for drinking. (9) So too is the milk of one whose calf has died or whose calf is another’s. (10) The milk of sheep, camels, and single-hoofed animals is unfit for drinking. (11) For drinking the milk of those animals that are unfit for consumption, one must perform the Kṛcchra penance, except in the case of cow's milk. (12) But for cow's milk, there is a fast for three nights. (13)

One may eat stale vegetable soup, meat broth, ghee, boiled grains, molasses, curd, honey, and parched grain flour, with the exception of [the first two]. Likewise, fermented liquids and molasses that has turned sour [are permitted]. 14–15.

Having performed the opening ceremony (*upākaraṇa*) on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa or Āṣāḍha, they should perform the concluding ceremony (*utsarga*) on the full moon day of Taiṣya or Māgha. They should conclude. 16.
Thus ends the twelfth section in the first book of the *Dharmasūtra* of Baudhāyana.
Thus ends the fifth chapter of the first book in the Dharma-sūtra of Baudhāyana.
The gods delight in a pure sacrifice. For the gods desire purity and are themselves pure. Regarding this, the following verse declares:
"O Maruts, for you who are pure, I present these pure oblations; I offer this pure sacrifice to the pure ones."
"By means of the cosmic order (ṛta), those who are bound by the cosmic order have come to truth; they are pure in birth, bright, and purifying. ||3||

New (unwashed) cloth is pure. Therefore, whatever is connected with a sacrifice, all that one should perform wearing unwashed garments. (4) The wife, the sacrificer, and the officiating priests should put on garments that have been washed, aired out, and are not worn out. (5) This applies from the commencement [of the rite] onwards. (6) It is likewise in long Soma sacrifices and in sacrificial sessions (sattras). (7) And it is according to what has been traditionally handed down. (8) As for instance, in the case of the *abhicaraṇīya* (malevolent) *iṣṭi*, animal, and Soma sacrifices, the officiating priests should proceed wearing red turbans and red garments; and in the *vṛṣākapi* [rite], they should wear variegated garments and variegated upper cloths. (9) At the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*), the garments should be made of linen; in their absence, they may be made of cotton or wool. (10)

11. For those [garments] defiled by urine, feces, blood, semen, and so forth, there is cleansing with earth and water. 12. As with clothing, so it is with *tārpya* and bark garments. 13. As with bark garments, so it is with black antelope skins (*kṛṣṇājina*). 14. A cloak that has been worn and put on must not be used without being washed. 15. One should not employ for divine purposes a garment that has been rinsed out but was previously associated with humans.

The defilement of solid ground is remedied by smearing it; 16. that of porous ground, by plowing it; 17. that of moist ground, by bringing pure earth and covering it over; 18. Ground is purified by four means: by treading upon it by cows, by digging, by burning, and by being rained upon; 19. and fifthly, by smearing; sixthly, by the lapse of time. 20.

21. Grass placed upon an unconsecrated ground must be washed. 22. Items defiled out of sight must be sprinkled with water. 23. The same applies to small fuel-sticks. 24. When large pieces of wood are defiled, they must be washed and dried. 25. But when many are defiled, they need only be sprinkled. 26. Wooden vessels that have come into contact with food-leavings must be scraped clean. 27. Those defiled by the sticking of food-leavings must be planed. 28. Those defiled by urine, feces, blood, semen, and the like must be discarded.

This [purification] is according to other specific instructions: [29] as in the case of the Agnihotra, the Gharma-remnant, the Dadhigharma, the Kuṇḍapāyinām Ayana, the Utsarginām Ayana, the Dākṣāyaṇayajña, the Iḍādadha, the Catuścakra, and the Brahmaudanas—in all these cases, the cleansing is performed with water and Darbha grass. [30] In all instances of consuming Soma, the cleansing on the Mārjālīya mound is performed with water alone. [31] In the case of defilement by urine, feces, blood, semen, and so forth, there is discarding [of the vessel]. [32]
Thus ends the thirteenth section in the first book of the *Dharmasūtra* of Baudhāyana.

1. Earthen vessels that have come into contact with food-leavings should be submerged. 2. Those defiled by the smearings of food-leavings should be fired again. 3. Those defiled by urine, feces, blood, semen, and the like should be discarded.

For metallic vessels that have been wiped clean as before, there shall be washing. (4) The materials for wiping are cow dung, earth, and ash. (5) For those [vessels] defiled by urine, feces, blood, semen, and so forth, there shall be remanufacture. (6) Alternatively, there shall be immersion for seven nights in cow urine or in a great river. (7) The same applies to vessels made of stone. (8)
The cleaning of *alābu*, *bilva*, and *vināla* with cow-hair; the washing of those woven from *naḷa*, bamboo, *śara*, and *kuśa* grass with cow-dung and water. ||9-10||

If rice grains are defiled, they should be washed and dried [if only a few]; if many, however, they should be sprinkled with water. If the husked rice is defiled, it should be discarded. The same applies to prepared sacrificial offerings (*siddhahavis*). If large quantities of food have been defiled by dogs, crows, or similar creatures, one should remove that portion of the food from that place and sprinkle the remainder with water while reciting the section beginning with *pavamānaḥ suvarjanaḥ*. Honey and liquids derived from milk become pure again when transferred from one vessel to another. Likewise, oil and clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*) should be placed in water and then used once they have been touched by something impure. If fire has been placed upon impure matter, one should re-establish the fire by churning and perform the *pavamāneṣṭi* sacrifice.

In the case of differences regarding purity, place, mantra, repetition, purpose, substance, preparation, and time, each preceding factor is more important than the one following it. Each preceding factor is more important. (19)
Thus ends the fourteenth section in the first book of the Dharmasūtra of Baudhāyana.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the first book of the *Dharmasūtra* of Baudhāyana.

The ritual procedure for the *vihāra* (Vedic study) is performed from left to right; likewise, the release [from the vow] is performed in that same manner. In rites for the ancestors (*pitrya*), the opposite is done. One should wash what has been struck by a foot. Having touched a limb or water from a skin-bag, one should touch water. In the same way, one should touch water after cutting, splitting, digging, spitting, or performing rites for the ancestors, for the *rakṣas*, for Nirṛti, for Rudra, or in exorcistic rites.

One should not protect oneself by means of a sacrificial implement accompanied by a mantra. (7) The internal components are the limbs of the sacrifice. (8) The external [components] are the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). (9) The wife and the sacrificer are more closely related to the sacrifice than the officiating priests. (10) Clarified butter (*ājya*) is closer to the limbs of the sacrifice than they are; the oblations (*havis*) are closer than the clarified butter; the animal victim is closer than the oblations; Soma is closer than the animal victim; and the fires are closer than Soma. (11)

The officiating priests shall not turn away from the sacrificial ground according to their respective duties. If he is facing east, he should turn toward his right shoulder; if facing west, toward his left.

The space between the *cātvāla* pit and the *utkara* heap is the sacrificial entrance (*tīrtha*). (15) Where there is no *cātvāla*, the *āhavanīya* fire and the *utkara* heap constitute it. (16) From there, the performers—the sacrificer and his wife—should enter. (17) This applies when the sacrifice has not yet concluded. (18) And when it has concluded, the movement [of the priests] is from the region of the *utkara*. (19)

One should not place upon the fire a piece of wood or a fuel-stick that has not been sprinkled with water, that has not been offered, or that is damp. (20) The Brahman and the sacrificer enter by the front of the Āhavanīya fire. (21) Some say they enter behind the Āhavanīya. (22) To the south of the Āhavanīya is the seat of the Brahman; to the west of that is the seat of the sacrificer. (23) To the north of the northern corner is the seat of the Hotṛ. (24) The mound for the rubbish is the seat of the Āgnīdhra. (25) Behind the Gārhapatya fire is the seat of the wife. (26) In these places, at each respective time, he spreads out Darbha grass. (27) A water-pot should be kept ready for each person for the purpose of sipping water. (28)

One who has undergone the consecration (*dīkṣita*) shall be endowed with the vow (*vrata*). (29) He shall not speak of another’s sin, he shall not become angry, and he shall not weep; he shall not look at urine or excrement. (30) Having seen something impure, he mutters: "The mind is unbound, the eye is poor; the Sun is the best of lights. O Consecration, do not abandon me! (31) Now, if it rains upon him, [he says]: "O flowing waters, bestow strength! Bestow vigor! Bestow strength! Do not destroy my consecration or my ascetic heat (*tapas*). (32)
Thus ends the fifteenth section in the first book of the *Dharmasūtra* of Baudhāyana.
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the first book of the Dharma-sūtra of Baudhāyana.

There are four castes: Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra. (1) According to the sequence of these castes, there are four wives for a Brāhmaṇa; (2) three for a Rājanya (Kṣatriya); (3) two for a Vaiśya; (4) and one for a Śūdra. (5)

Among them, sons born of women of the same caste or of the next lower caste are of the same caste as their fathers. (6) Sons born of women one or two castes lower are Ambaṣṭhas, Ugras, and Niṣādas respectively. (7) Sons born of women in the reverse order of castes are Āyogavas, Māgadhas, Vaiṇas, Kṣattṛs, Pulkasas, Kukkuṭas, Vaidehakas, and Caṇḍālas. (8)

From an Ambaṣṭha on a woman of the first [caste], a Śvapāka is born; from an Ugra on a woman of the second, a Vaiṇa; from a Niṣāda on a woman of the third, a Pulkasa; and in the reverse order, a Kukkuṭa.

A son born of a Niṣāda father and a Niṣāda mother by one who is himself a Niṣāda removes the status of a Śūdra up to the fifth generation. One should initiate him at the sixth generation and allow him to perform sacrifices. The seventh generation is called *avikṛtabīja* (of unaltered seed), the eighth *samabīja* (of equal seed), and the ninth *sama* (equal); these designations apply in successive order.

Those whom a man who has not observed his vows begets through women of the three [upper] castes because of their similarity [to himself], the wise call them *vrātyas*, those who have fallen away from the *Sāvitrī*.
"The wise call them *vrātyas*," so it is said. (16)
Thus ends the sixteenth section in the first book of the Baudhāyana Dharmasūtra.
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the first book of the Dharmasūtra of Baudhāyana.

The Rathakāra, Ambaṣṭha, Sūta, Ugra, Māgadha, Āyogava, Vaiṇa, Kṣattṛ, Pulkasa, Kukkuṭa, Vaidehaka, Caṇḍāla, Śvapāka, and so forth. (1) Among them, from those of the same caste, children of the same caste are born. (2) From a Brāhmaṇa, on a Kṣatriya woman, a Brāhmaṇa is born; on a Vaiśya woman, an Ambaṣṭha; on a Śūdra woman, a Niṣāda. (3) Some say he is a Pāraśava. (4) From a Kṣatriya, on a Vaiśya woman, a Kṣatriya is born; on a Śūdra woman, an Ugra. (5) From a Vaiśya, on a Śūdra woman, a Rathakāra is born. (6)

From a Śūdra, with a Vaiśya woman, a Māgadha is born; with a Kṣatriya woman, a Kṣattṛ; and with a Brāhmaṇa woman, a Caṇḍāla. From a Vaiśya, with a Kṣatriya woman, an Āyogava is born; with a Brāhmaṇa woman, a Vaidehaka. From a Kṣatriya, with a Brāhmaṇa woman, a Sūta is born.
In that regard, from the union of an Ambaṣṭha man and an Ugrā woman, an Anuloma is born; from the union of a Kṣattṛ man and a Vaidehaka woman, a Pratiloma is born.

From an Ugra born of a Kṣatriya woman comes a Śvapāka (11). From a Vaidehaka born of an Ambaṣṭha woman comes a Vaiṇa (12). From a Niṣāda born of a Śūdra woman comes a Pulkasa (13). From a Śūdra born of a Niṣāda woman comes a Kukkuṭa (14).
The wise call those born from the intermixture of castes *vrātyas*;
the wise call them *vrātyas*. (15)
Thus ends the seventeenth section in the first book of the Baudhāyana Dharmasūtra.
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the first book of the Baudhāyana Dharmasūtra.
The king, who receives a sixth part [as tax], shall protect his subjects. ||1||

Brahman indeed placed his own majesty within the Brāhmaṇas, joined with study, teaching, sacrificing, officiating at sacrifices, giving, and receiving, for the protection of the Vedas. (2) He placed strength within the Kṣatriyas, joined with study, sacrificing, giving, weapons, armor, and the protection of beings, for the prosperity of the Kṣatra. (3) He placed [strength] within the Vaiśyas, joined with study, sacrificing, giving, agriculture, trade, and cattle-rearing, for the prosperity of their occupations. (4) He placed service to the former [classes] among the Śūdras. (5) For they were created from the feet. (6)
One should appoint a domestic priest who is capable in all respects; one should abide by his instruction.

He shall not turn back from battle. (9) He shall not strike with hollow-pointed arrows nor with poisoned ones. (10) He shall not fight with those who are terrified, intoxicated, insane, or deranged; nor with those who are unarmored, women, children, the elderly, or Brahmins. (11) Except in the case of an assassin. (12) Furthermore, they cite this: "If one kills an assassin who has come to his family as a teacher, he does not thereby become a killer of an embryo; for fury recoils upon fury. (13)

For maritime goods, having extracted the best portion, the customs duty shall be one hundred paṇas for every ten paṇas [of value]. For other goods as well, he shall fix a lawful rate in accordance with their intrinsic worth, without causing injury [to the merchants].
After having guarded for one year the property of a non-Brāhmaṇa whose owner has disappeared, the king may take it. ||16||

A Brāhmaṇa is indeed not to be killed for any offense whatsoever. (17) In the case of a Brāhmaṇa who commits the murder of a Brāhmaṇa, sexual intercourse with the teacher’s wife, theft of gold, or the drinking of liquor, he shall be branded on the forehead with heated iron with the marks of a vulva, a female organ, a jackal, or a tavern-sign, and then banished from the realm. (18)

In the case of killing a Brāhmaṇa, the punishment for Kṣatriyas and others shall be death and the confiscation of all their property. (19) For killing those same persons when they are of equal or inferior status, one should prescribe appropriate punishments according to their respective strength. (20)
Thus ends the eighteenth section in the first book of the Dharma-sūtra of Baudhāyana.

For the killing of a Kṣatriya, one should present to the king a thousand cows with an additional bull for the purpose of avenging the enmity. (1) For a Vaiśya, a hundred; for a Śūdra, ten, and in this case an additional bull. (2) By the rule for the killing of a Śūdra, the killing of a woman and the killing of a cow are explained; however, this excludes the killing of an Ātreyī woman, a milch-cow, and a draft-ox. (3) In the case of killing a milch-cow or a draft-ox, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance at the end [of the period]. (4) The killing of an Ātreyī woman is explained by the rule for the killing of a Kṣatriya. (5) For the killing of a swan, a vulture, a peacock, a ruddy goose, a heron, a crow, an owl, a frog, a *ḍiḍḍika*, a *ḍerikā*, a dog, a mongoose, a mongoose-cat, and so forth, the penance is like that for a Śūdra. (6)
For the sake of maintaining social order, one should give testimony exactly as it was seen or heard. ||7||
One quarter of the unrighteousness falls upon the perpetrator; one quarter goes to the witness;
one quarter falls upon all the members of the court; and one quarter reaches the king.
The king becomes free from sin, and the members of the assembly are also released;
the guilt goes to the perpetrator where the one deserving of blame is indeed blamed. (8)
And having thus designated a witness, the discerning judge should question him with diligence. ||9||
On the night you were born and on the night you shall die—
whatever good deed you have performed during the interval between these two, all that would go to the king if you speak a falsehood. (10)
A witness who speaks falsely in testimony destroys three fathers and three grandfathers, as well as seven generations—both those already born and those yet unborn. (11)
By speaking falsehood for the sake of gold, one destroys three generations of ancestors;
by falsehood regarding small cattle, one destroys five; and by falsehood regarding cows, one destroys ten.
One kills a hundred horses by lying regarding a horse; one kills a thousand men by lying regarding a man; but by lying regarding land, a witness who speaks falsely destroys everything. (12)

Members of the four castes who have sons may serve as witnesses, with the exception of those who are Vedic scholars (*śrotriya*), kings, renunciants, and those deficient in human qualities. (13) In the case of a transgression against the *Smṛti*, the penance is determined primarily by the specific rule [prescribed therein]. (14) Otherwise, there shall be the punishment of being cut down like a tree. (15) "One should drink hot milk for twelve nights, or one should offer oblations with the *Kūṣmāṇḍa* hymns"—thus it is said; "or one should offer oblations with the *Kūṣmāṇḍa* hymns. (16)
Thus ends the nineteenth section in the first book of the Baudhāyana Dharmasūtra.
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the first book of the Baudhāyana Dharmasūtra.

There are eight forms of marriage. 1. Having ascertained [the bride’s] learning and character, if she is given to a student who asks for her, that is the *brāhma* form. 2. Having clothed and adorned her, saying, "Let him perform his duty together with her," it is the *prājāpatya* form. 3. After first having offered the oblation of parched grain (*lājāhuti*), if she is given along with two cows, it is the *ārṣa* form. 4. When the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) are being led away, if she is given to the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) within the sacrificial enclosure (*antarvedi*), that is the *daiva* form. 5. If she is gratified by wealth, it is the *āsura* form. 6. The mutual union of one who desires her with one who desires him is the *gāndharva* form. 7. By abduction by force, it is the *rākṣasa* form. 8. If he approaches her while she is asleep, intoxicated, or mentally deranged, it is the *paiśāca* form. 9. Thus there are nine forms. (Note: The text lists eight, but the traditional count is nine; the ninth is often included in the list above.)

Of these, four belong to the Brāhmaṇa; among them, each preceding one is superior to the next. (10) Among the latter [four], each succeeding one is more base than the preceding. (11) Even here, the sixth and seventh follow the duties of the Kṣatriya, because the Kṣatriya is dependent upon them. (12) The fifth and eighth belong to the Vaiśya and the Śūdra respectively. (13) For the Vaiśya and the Śūdra have wives who are not constrained by strict rules. (14) This is because they are primarily occupied with agriculture and service. (15) Some, moreover, praise even the Gāndharva form of marriage for all classes, as it is characterized by mutual affection. (16)
Thus ends the twentieth section in the first book of the Dharma-sūtra of Baudhāyana.
"It is known that as the marriage is contracted, so the offspring becomes. Furthermore, they also cite this:
"A woman who has been purchased with wealth is not ordained as a wife;
she is neither for the rites to the gods nor for the rites to the ancestors; Kāśyapa declared her to be a slave-girl."
Those who, deluded by greed, bestow their own daughter for a bride-price are sellers of themselves— sinful men who commit a great transgression.
They fall into a terrible hell and destroy their lineage unto the seventh generation;
indeed, all coming and going is prescribed as a toll.

On the full moon day, the eighth day (*aṣṭakā*), the new moon day, during fires, portents, earthquakes, at a cremation ground, when the ruler or a learned *śrotriya* departs, and when one sets out on a journey, there is no study for a day and a night. (4) During a wind that carries a foul odor, in mist, and while the sounds of dancing, singing, instrumental music, weeping, or the *sāman* chants are heard, [there is no study] for as long as those conditions persist. (5) When thunder, rain, and lightning occur together, there is no study for three days, except during the rainy season. (6) Even during the rainy season, excluding the time of actual rain, there is no study for a day and a night at those specific times. (7)

And for one who has accepted a gift from a paternal relative or has eaten [at such a meal], the impurity lasts for the remainder of that day. (8) Regarding meals, the impurity lasts until digestion. (9) For the Brāhmaṇa is indeed "one whose hand is his mouth. (10) Moreover, they cite this:
"The Śruti declares that what is eaten and what is accepted as a gift are indistinguishable. (11)

When the father has died, [the impurity lasts] for three nights. (12) Now, there are indeed two kinds of seed belonging to a learned Brāhmaṇa named Suśravas: one above the navel and the other below it. That which is above the navel—by means of that he procreates when he initiates Brāhmaṇas, when he teaches them, when he performs sacrifices for them, and when he does what is good. All this constitutes his offspring. Then, that which is below the navel—by means of that his own biological offspring is produced. Therefore, they do not say of a learned man who has mastered the Vedas, "You are childless. (13) Therefore, a Brāhmaṇa is called by two names, has two faces, possesses two kinds of seed, and is twice-born. (14)
And for as long as one hears or sees a *śūdra* or an outcaste (*apapātra*), [one should not study]. (15) One should not study at night when a jackal howls, until one falls asleep. (16)

One should not study during the day and night, at the two twilights, or on the days of the lunar changes (parvan). (17) One should not eat meat, nor should one approach a woman. (18) For it is known that on the days of the lunar changes, Rākṣasas and Piśācas become prone to transgression. (19)

On account of other extraordinary portents, there is no study for a day and night, except for mental recitation. (20) Even in the case of mental recitation, there is no study during births or deaths. (21)
Moreover, they cite this:
"The eighth day destroys the teacher; the fourteenth day destroys the pupil;
the fifteenth day destroys knowledge. Therefore, one should avoid [studying] on these sacred festival days."
Therefore, one should avoid [sexual intercourse] on the festival days. ||22||
Thus ends the twenty-first section in the first book of the Baudhāyana Dharmasūtra.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the first book of the *Dharmasūtra* of Baudhāyana.
Thus ends the first inquiry.
Now, therefore, follow the expiations. 1.

A killer of a learned Brahmin (*bhrūṇahan*) shall [perform penance] for twelve years. (2) Carrying a skull and a staff (*khaṭvāṅga*), clothed in the skin of a donkey, making his dwelling in the forest, he should construct a hut in a cremation ground, using a corpse's head as a banner. He should live there, wandering for alms at seven houses while proclaiming his own deed, and sustain his life by that; if he receives nothing, he shall fast. (3) Or he may sacrifice with the Aśvamedha, the Gosava, or the Agniṣṭut. (4) Or he may immerse himself in the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of the Aśvamedha. (5) Furthermore, they cite this: "By killing a Brahmin unintentionally, one becomes defiled according to the Dharma. (6)
The sages declare that there is atonement for killing unintentionally;
for one who kills intentionally, no atonement is found.
If one threatens another, one should perform the Kṛcchra penance; if one strikes them down, the Atikṛcchra.
If blood flows, one must perform both the Kṛcchra and the Cāndrāyaṇa.
Therefore, one should never threaten anyone, nor should one cause blood to flow. ||7||
Nine years for a Rājanya; eight for a Vaiśya; one year for a Śūdra; and likewise for a woman. For an Ātreyī, it is as for a Brāhmaṇa.

One who has violated the bed of his guru shall lie upon a heated iron bed (13); or he shall embrace a glowing metal image (sūrmi) (14); or, having cut off his penis together with the testicles and holding them in his cupped hands, he shall walk toward the intermediate direction between south and west until he collapses (15).

A thief, having disheveled his hair and taken a club made of *saidhraka* wood upon his shoulder, should go to the king saying, "Slay me with this! He shall slay him with it. Furthermore, they cite this:
"Taking a club upon his shoulder, a thief should follow the king, saying:
'O King, remembering the duty of a Kṣatriya, punish me with this!'"
Whether in the punishment or in the release of a thief, he is freed from the guilt;
but by failing to punish him, the king incurs that guilt from the thief. (17)

Having drunk *surā*, one should burn the body with hot [liquor]. (18) If one drinks it unintentionally, one should perform the *kṛcchra* penance for one-fourth of a year and undergo initiation again. (19) Furthermore, there is no lapse of the shaving, the vows, or the observances, because they have already been performed previously. (20) Moreover, they cite this: "A Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, or a Vaiśya who has unintentionally drunk *vāruṇī* liquor, or has consumed urine or feces, deserves to undergo the purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) once more. (21)
But he who drinks water that has stood overnight in a vessel used for storing liquor shall subsist on milk boiled with Śaṅkhapuṣpī for six days.
If one dies while being administered treatment by a teacher, the teacher shall perform three *kṛcchra* penances. This same rule applies in the case of one who has not been consecrated.

A student (*brahmacārin*) does not break his vow by performing the funeral rites for anyone other than his mother, father, or teacher. (25) If he should fall ill, he may at will eat all the remnants of his teacher’s food for the sake of medicine. (26) He may be treated with whatever remedy he desires. (27) When he has recovered, he rises and worships the sun with this verse: "The swan dwelling in purity... (RV 4.40.5). (28)

Having emitted semen during the day, one should drink water that reaches the heart three times with the *retasyā* verses. (29) A student who approaches a woman is an *avakīrṇin*. (30) He should sacrifice a donkey as the victim. (31) The victim and the sacrificial cake belong to Nirṛti; they may also belong to the Rakṣases or to Yama. (32) It is known from tradition: "They perform the ritual with the portions [of the victim], including the *prāśitra*, over water, starting from the penis. (33) Alternatively, on the night of the new moon, having kindled the fire and performed the preliminary rites for a wood-oblation (*dārvihomika*), he offers two oblations of clarified butter: "Desire has made me an *avakīrṇin*; I am an *avakīrṇin*, O Desire! To Desire, svāhā! "I have been betrayed by Desire; I am betrayed, O Desire! To Desire, svāhā! (34) Having offered the oblations, with hands joined in reverence, he should address the fire from a side position.
"May the Maruts sprinkle me; may Indra sprinkle me; may Bṛhaspati sprinkle me;
may this Agni sprinkle me with long life and with strength—make me long-lived! ||35||

Then his relatives, in the assembly, should pour out a vessel of water, saying, "I am so-and-so, being such-and-such. Having performed [the penance], when he has begun to consume water, milk, ghee, honey, and salt, the Brahmins should say to him, "Have you completed the penance? The other replies, "Yes. They should then perform for him the *savanīya* sacrifice which fulfills the requirement of the penance.

If he should unknowingly approach a woman of the same lineage, he should support her as if she were his mother. If she has given birth, he should perform a quarter of a year-long *kṛcchra* penance and offer oblations with these two [verses]: "Whatever defilement has come upon me" and "Agni has given back my sight."
The superseded elder brother, the one who marries before him, she whom he thus marries, as well as the giver and the officiating priest—these five all go to hell. (39)

The one superseded, the superseder, the giver [of the girl], and he who performs the sacrifice—all these are purified by a twelve-night kṛcchra penance; a woman is purified by a three-night penance. ||40||
Thus ends the first section in the second book of the Dharma-sūtra of Baudhāyana.

Now, the acts causing loss of caste (*patanīya*): [1] sailing upon the ocean; [2] misappropriating a deposit of sacred property belonging to a Brahmin; [3] false testimony regarding land; [4] trading in all types of merchandise; [5] serving a Śūdra; [6] being born of a Śūdra woman; [7] and having offspring from such a union. Having committed any one of these—[9].
They should eat sparingly at the fourth mealtime and descend into water according to the ritual of the Soma-pressings;
they should pass their time alternating between standing and sitting.
They destroy that evil in three years. ||10||
Whatever black sin a Brahmin commits by associating with the dark caste for a single night, he may purify it by eating only at every fourth mealtime and subsisting on water.
In three years, he destroys that evil. ||11||

Now, the minor offenses (upapātaka): 12. Having sexual intercourse with those who should not be approached—such as the wife of a teacher, the female friend of a teacher, a woman who has lost her caste, or one who has fallen from grace; practicing medicine; officiating at sacrifices for a village; subsisting by the stage; being a teacher of acting; tending cattle and buffaloes; and whatever else is of a similar nature, such as defiling a maiden. 13.
But their expiation consists of living like an outcast for two years. 14.

Now, the acts that cause impurity: [15] gambling, performing malevolent magic, living by gleaning for one who has not maintained the sacred fires, wandering for alms after having returned home from studentship, remaining in the teacher's house beyond four months, teaching him [beyond that period], and the pointing out of constellations. [16]

The expiation for these, however, consists of twelve months, twelve half-months, twelve periods of twelve days, twelve periods of six days, twelve periods of three days, twelve days, six days, three days, one day and night, or one day, according to the repetition of the offense. 17.

Now, those who have fallen, having come together, should practice their duties as mutual sacrificers, mutual teachers, and marrying one another. Having produced sons, they should say to them: "Depart from us; in this way you will attain the status of the noble. Furthermore, one does not fall along with his organs. This is to be understood by the following: even one who is deficient in a limb may procreate a son who possesses all limbs.

Hārīta says this is false. Women should be like a curd-pot: for when one who is impure churns milk that has been curdled in a curd-pot, the learned do not employ it for religious rites. Likewise, there is no association with that which is produced from an impure seed.

For those born of impure semen, expiation is prescribed according to their desire [to perform it]. For those who have committed a sin causing loss of caste (*patanīya*), women receive a third part; for women, the share is a third.
Moreover, they cite this:
"Whatever else one does with sesame seeds other than giving them as food or for anointing the body, having become a worm in a dog's excrement, one sinks down together with one's ancestors. (26)

He who sells sesame seeds sells his ancestors; he who sells rice grains sells his vital breaths; and he who, for the sake of profit, gives away his daughter in marriage, sells his shares of merit. (27) Grass and wood that have not been processed may be sold. Furthermore, they cite this:
"One-tusked animals, stone extracted from salt-mines, and thread dyed with indigo—these, O Brāhmaṇa, are your articles of trade. (28–29)

Or, excluding the most heinous sins (*pātaka*), one should give a brownish-tawny cow with thick hair, having sprinkled it with clarified butter and scattered it with black sesame seeds, to a man learned in the Vedas (*anūcāna*). Or, for twelve days, by means of the *Kūśmāṇḍa* formulas; thereby one is released from whatever sin has been committed prior to the killing of a learned Brahmin (*bhrūṇahatyā*).
For falsely accusing someone of a mortal sin (pātaka), the penance is a Kṛcchra; for the accuser, it is a year-long [penance].
One becomes an outcast by associating with an outcast for a year through officiating at sacrifices, teaching, or marriage; but not through sharing a vehicle, a seat, or food. (35)
For consuming impure substances, the penance is the *naiṣpurīṣya* rite; that is accomplished within seven nights.

37. Drinking hot water, milk, ghee, and air, each for three days respectively, constitutes the *taptakṛcchra*. 38. Eating [only] in the morning for three days, likewise in the evening for three days, and eating only what is unasked for (unsolicited) for three days—this is the *kṛcchra*. 39. Eating in the morning for three nights, in the evening for three nights, and eating what is unsolicited for three nights—these three periods of four nights constitute the *kṛcchra* for women, children, and the elderly. 40. One should eat only as much as one can take in a single mouthful; as before, this is the *atikṛcchra*. 41. Subsisting on water alone is the third; that is the *kṛcchrātikṛcchra*.

In the Kṛcchra penance, there is bathing with water three times a day; sleeping on the ground; wearing a single garment; and shaving the hair of the head, the beard, the body hair, and the nails. This same rule applies to women as well, with the exception of shaving the hair. This is with the exception of shaving the hair.
Thus ends the second section of the second book in the Dharma Sūtra of Baudhāyana.
Thus ends the first chapter of the second book in the Dharma-sūtra of Baudhāyana.

One who constantly uses water for purification, constantly wears the sacred thread, constantly engages in Vedic study, avoids the food of a *vṛṣala*, approaches his wife only during her season, and offers oblations according to the rules— [is not defiled by the death of a relative].
A true Brahmin does not fall from the world of Brahmā. ||1||

"The Vedic tradition states: 'Manu divided his inheritance among his sons. (2) It was an equal division for all, because there was no distinction made. (3) Or rather, the eldest may set aside a choice portion according to its quality. (4) For the Vedic tradition says: 'Therefore, they cause the eldest son to depart with a share of the wealth. (5) Or, the eldest may set aside one [share] from ten. (6) The others shall divide the remainder equally. (7)
The partition of the inheritance takes place with the father's consent while the father is still living. ||8||
Among the four castes, cattle, horses, goats, and sheep constitute the senior share. 9.

In the case of a collection of wives and sons of various castes, they shall divide the inheritance by making ten parts, distributing them in order as four, three, two, and one [parts] respectively. (10) But when a son of the body (aurasa) is born, those of equal caste are entitled to a third part. (11) Between a son of equal caste and a son of a woman of the next lower caste, if the son of the next lower caste is virtuous, he shall take the share of the eldest. (12) For a virtuous son becomes the supporter of the rest. (13)
One should know that a son begotten by oneself upon a consecrated wife of equal caste is an *aurasa* (legitimate) son.
Moreover, they cite this [verse]:
"You arise from limb after limb; you are born from the heart."
"You are indeed the self named 'son'; live for a hundred autumns. ||14||
Having accepted that what is born from a daughter is the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikāputra*), and that any other [son born of her] is a daughter's son (*dauhitra*). ||15||
Moreover, they also cite this: "The son of an appointed daughter should assign the mother at the first pinda, her father at the second, and her grandfather at the third. (16)

He who is begotten on a deceased man, or on one who is impotent or diseased, by another with the consent [of the owner] on his own wife, is a *kṣetraja* son. He has two fathers and two gotras, and he becomes a sharer in the funeral offerings (*svadhā*) and the inheritance of both. Furthermore, they cite this: "There should be an offering of rice balls (*piṇḍa*) for two fathers; on each rice ball, the names of both should be mentioned.
There should thus be three rice balls for six [ancestors]; acting in this way, one does not go astray. (17–19)

One who is given by both parents, or by either one, and is accepted for the sake of offspring, is a *datta* (given) son. ||20|| One whom [the father], being of similar status and desiring it, himself makes his own, is an *kṛtrima* (adopted) son. ||21|| One born secretly in the house and recognized at the end is a *gūḍhaja* (secretly born) son. ||22|| One who is abandoned by both parents, or by either one, and is accepted for the sake of offspring, is an *apaviddha* (cast-off) son. ||23|| The son born of a woman whom one approaches when she is unmarried and not given away [in marriage] is a *kānīna* (maiden-born) son. ||24|| The son born of a woman who is married while pregnant—whether her pregnancy was known or unknown—is a *sahoḍha* (born with the bride) son. ||25|| One who is purchased from the hands of both parents, or from either one, and is accepted for the sake of offspring, is a *krīta* (bought) son. ||26|| The son born of a *punarbhū* (a remarried woman)—she who, having abandoned a eunuch or an outcast husband, finds another husband—is a *paunarbhava* (son of a remarried woman). ||27|| One who, being deprived of both parents, gives himself up of his own accord, is a *svayaṃdatta* (self-given) son. ||28|| One born to a Śūdra woman from a preeminent member of the twice-born classes is a *niṣāda*. ||29|| From lust, he is called a *pāraśava*; these are the sons. ||30||
Moreover, they cite this example:

"The son of the body, the son of an appointed daughter, the son born of the wife, the given son, the made son, the son born in secret, and the cast-off son—these are declared to be the sharers of the inheritance. (31)

The son born of an unmarried girl (kānīna), the son received with a bride (sahoḍha), the purchased son (krīta), the son of a remarried woman (paunarbhava), the self-given son (svayaṃdatta), and the Niṣāda— these they declare to be sharers of the family name.
"Aupajaṅghani says that among those [theories], it is only the first one."
O Father, I do not envy women now as I did before,
because they have declared that in the abode of Yama, one speaks of the son as belonging to the progenitor.
The progenitor of the seed leads the son away after death to the abode of Yama;
therefore, fearing the seed of another, men guard their wives. (34)
Be vigilant and guard this lineage; let not others sow their seeds in your field.
In the life hereafter, a son belongs to the one who begot him.
"The knower acts in vain upon this thread," so it is said. ||35||

They shall deposit the shares of those who have not yet attained legal capacity, along with their increments, in secure custody until they reach the age of majority. (36) They shall maintain those whose legal capacity has expired, as well as the blind, the mentally infirm, the impotent, those addicted to vices, the diseased, and so forth, by providing food and clothing. (37–38) This applies to those incapable of performing work. (39) Excepting, however, those who have fallen from caste and their offspring. (40)
No social interaction with those who have fallen [from their caste] is permitted. However, one should support even a mother who has fallen, provided one does not speak with her.
Daughters may receive their mother’s ornaments, whether they were handed down traditionally or otherwise. (43) No independence exists for a woman. (44) Furthermore, they cite this:
"The father protects her in childhood; the husband protects her in youth; the son protects her in old age. A woman does not deserve independence. (45)
"For women are considered to be without sense-faculties and without inheritance; such is the sacred tradition. ||46||

Striving for the welfare of their husband, they shall conquer the heavenly world. (47) In the event of a transgression, a *kṛcchra* penance is required. (48) In the case of a *śūdra*, one should perform the *cāndrāyaṇa*. (49) Among those beginning with the *vaiśya*, one should perform the *kṛcchrātikṛcchra* and other penances in reverse order [of the castes]. (50) For men of the *brāhmaṇa* and other castes, there shall be a year-long period of celibacy (*brahmacarya*). (51) One should burn a *śūdra* with a fire of straw mats (*kaṭāgni*). (52)
Moreover, they also cite this: ||53||
Thus ends the third section in the second book of the Dharma-sūtra of Baudhāyana.
For a non-Brāhmaṇa who commits adultery, corporal punishment shall be the penalty. ||1||
For all social classes alike, one's wife is more worthy of protection than wealth. ||2||
But there is no execution for those in the wives of wandering performers, nor on the stage;
for they cause these men to disperse, yet they also make them perform while they are well-guarded. (3)
Women are an incomparable means of purification; they are never defiled.
For month after month, their menstrual flow carries away all impurities.
Soma gave them purity, Gandharva taught them speech, and Agni granted them the power to consume all things; therefore, women are free from blemish.
One should abandon a wife who bears no children in the tenth year, one whose children are all female in the twelfth year,
one whose children die in the fifteenth year, but one who speaks unpleasantly immediately.

For one year, the wife of a deceased man shall avoid honey, meat, liquor, and salt, and sleep on the ground. Maudgalya says it is for six months. After this period, being permitted by her elders, she may, if she is childless, procreate a son with her brother-in-law.

Moreover, they cite this example: "A barren woman, one whose sons have already been born, one who has ceased to menstruate, and one whose offspring have passed away—none of these should be employed against her will, for no fruit exists in them. (10)

A maternal uncle’s wife, a father’s sister, a sister, a daughter-in-law, a nephew’s wife, a maternal aunt, and a friend’s wife—these are women who must not be approached for sexual intercourse. (11) For approaching those women who must not be approached, the penance is the Kṛcchrātikṛcchra and the Cāndrāyaṇa. (12) By this, sexual intercourse with a Caṇḍāla woman is explained. (13) Moreover, they cite this:
"A Brāhmaṇa who, through ignorance, has intercourse with a Caṇḍāla woman, eats her food, or accepts gifts from her, falls from his status; but if he does so knowingly, he becomes equal [to her]. (14)
