By approaching through negligence the wife of one's father, teacher, or king, one becomes a violator of the guru’s bed; the atonement for this has been stated previously. ||15||

If he is unable [to subsist] by teaching, officiating at sacrifices, or receiving gifts, he may live according to the duty of a Kṣatriya, because that is the next in order. "Not so," says Gautama; "for the duty of a Kṣatriya is exceedingly fierce for a Brāhmaṇa. Moreover, they cite this example: "For the sake of a cow, for the sake of a Brāhmaṇa, or even in the event of a confusion of castes, a Brāhmaṇa and a Vaiśya may take up arms out of regard for dharma."

The livelihood of a Vaiśya should be followed because it is the next in order. (19) Before breakfast, he should be a cultivator. (20) [He should plough] with two bulls whose noses have not been pierced and whose testicles are intact, without piercing them with a goad, repeatedly encouraging them by shouting. (21)

The fire [is that] beginning with the wife; in that [fire], the performance of rites takes place prior to the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*). From the establishment of the sacred fires onwards, however, these [rites] become perpetual: namely, the establishment of the sacred fires, the *agnihotra*, the new- and full-moon sacrifices, the *āgrayaṇa*, the animal sacrifice during the northern and southern solstices, the four-monthly sacrifices at the beginning of each season, the *ṣaḍḍhotṛ* offering, and the *jyotiṣṭoma* in spring—thus [constitutes] the attainment of security. Moreover, they cite this:
"Neither by one habituated to sleeping by day, nor by one who eats all kinds of food, nor by one who has fallen from his high station, is it possible to reach heaven at will. (24)
One should avoid meanness, deceit, and laziness. Furthermore, in this regard, they cite a verse from the dialogue between Uśanas and the two daughters of Vṛṣaparvan:
"You are indeed the daughter of one who praises, begs, and accepts;
whereas I am the son of one who is praised, gives, and does not accept."
"Of one who gives, there is no recipient. ||26||
Thus ends the fourth section in the second book of the Dharma-sūtra of Baudhāyana.
Thus ends the second chapter of the second book in the Dharma-sūtra of Baudhāyana.

Austerity consists of plunging into the waters. (1) Having gratified the deities, he performs the libation for the ancestors. (2) He pours out water along the bank of the river with the verse: "Carrying strength... (3). Now they also cite this: "In flowing rivers that are not obstructed, members of the three twice-born classes, having risen in the morning, should perform the libations for the gods, the sages, and the ancestors. (4)
When [the works] have been completed, those who built the bridge shall not claim a share therein. //5//
Therefore, one should avoid bridges and wells made by others. ||6||
Moreover, they cite this example:

"Or, having extracted three lumps of earth, one should perform [the rite] in times of distress, but not always; however, when [water] is obstructed, one should likewise take three lumps of earth from a well and three jars of water. (7)

"Having accepted what should not be accepted, or having accepted what may be accepted, or having officiated at a sacrifice for one for whom one should not officiate, or having eaten the food of one whose food should not be eaten, one should mutter the *taratsamandīya* [verses]. (8) Moreover, they also cite this:
"Those who cause confusion among gurus, those who cause confusion among disciples, and those who cause confusion regarding food and mantras—these dwell in long-lasting darkness. (9)
Now follow the observances of the Snātaka. 10.

In the evening and in the morning, having offered the Vaiśvadeva bali with whatever food is fit for eating, he should honor Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras who have arrived as guests according to his ability. (11) If he is unable to provide for many, he should give to one who possesses good qualities. (12) Or [he may give] to whoever has arrived first. (13) If a Śūdra has arrived, he should employ him in work. (14) Or he should give the best portion to one learned in the Vedas (śrotriya). (15)

A distribution [of food] is ordained for those who are constant devotees, provided it does not cause them hardship. (16) But one must never eat without having first given [to others]. (17) Furthermore, regarding this, they cite two verses from the *Anna-gītā*:
"He who eats me [as food] without having first offered me to the ancestors, the deities, servants, guests, and his circle of friends..."
Eating what is prepared, he eats poison through delusion;
him I devour, and I am his death.

He who has offered the agnihotra oblation, performed the vaiśvadeva rite, honored his guests, and— being contented, pure, and full of faith— eats what remains after the servants have been fed, eats me.
In that [state] I shall become immortal, and he protects me. ||18||

A distribution of goods according to one's ability should be made to excellent Brahmins who are learned in the Vedas and have mastered them, for the sake of their teacher, for the purpose of a marriage, for medicine, for those whose livelihood is exhausted, for one about to perform a sacrifice, for one engaged in Vedic study, for one on a journey, and for a Vaiśvajit; provided they are begging outside the sacrificial altar. To others, cooked food should be given.

Having thoroughly washed his hands and feet and sipped water for purification, he should take the food brought to him in a clean, enclosed place; having cast away desire, anger, malice, greed, and delusion, he should eat with all his fingers, making no sound.
Thus ends the fifth section in the second book of the Baudhāyana Dharmasūtra.

One should not discard the remnants of a meal in the alms-bowl. (1) If one consumes meat, fish, or sesame mixed with food, one should sip water and touch fire. (2) And one should bathe after sunset. (3) One should avoid using a seat made of *pālāśa* wood, sandals, or a tooth-stick. (4) One should not eat food placed on one's lap. (5) One should not eat while sitting on a chair. (6)

He should carry a staff made of *vaiṇava* wood and wear earrings of gold. (7) He should avoid washing one foot with the other and avoid standing upon it. (8) He should not wear a garland outside his garment. (9) He should not look at the sun at its rising or setting. (10) He should not point out a rainbow to another person. (11) If he must speak of it, he should say "the jewel-bow" (*maṇidhanus*). (12) He should not pass between the gateposts and the crossbar of a city gate. (13) He should not walk between the two side-beams of a swing. (14) He should not walk over a rope tethering calves. (15) He should not step on ashes, bones, hair, chaff, potsherds, or bathing-remnants. (16)

One should not point out a cow suckling her calf to another person. (17) One should not call a milch cow "non-milch. (18) If one must speak of it, one should say, "she is about to become a milch cow. (19) One should not utter words that are sour, harsh, or rough. (20)
One should not travel alone on a road. (21) Not with those who have fallen [from their caste], nor with a woman, nor with a Śūdra. (22) One should not travel at evening. (23)

One should not bathe naked. (24) One should not bathe at night. (25) One should not cross a river by swimming with one's arms. (26) One should not look down into a well. (27) One should not look down into a pit. (28) One should not sit in a place where another person would have to lift him up. (29)
The way must be yielded to a Brahmin, a cow, a king, one who is sightless, an elder, one afflicted by heat, a pregnant woman, and one who is weak. (30)

A righteous person should strive to dwell in a village that has an abundance of firewood, water, fodder, fuel, kusha grass, and garlands; one that is easy to exit, crowded with wealthy people, prosperous with industries, filled mostly with noble folk, and not accessible to bandits. (31)
A Brahmin who lives for twelve years in a village whose water supply is a single well, while being the husband of a Śūdra woman, attains the same status as a Śūdra. (32)
With his body covered by the dust of the city, his eyes and face completely filled with it, though dwelling in the city with a well-restrained self, he will not attain perfection—this is not so. (33)
The dust raised by chariots, horses, elephants, grain, and cows is auspicious;
however, that raised by a broom, dogs, goats, sheep, donkeys, and clothes is inauspicious.
One should honor those worthy of honor. ||35||

Sages, learned men, the best of kings, maternal uncles, fathers-in-law, and officiating priests—these are declared by the scriptures to be worthy of the arghya offering according to the divisions of time. (36)
At the commencement of the rite, the sage, the learned man, and the king are obtained as the excellent officiating priests;
likewise, the maternal uncle and the father-in-law are to be honored when they arrive or depart within the course of a year. ||37||
In the fire-sanctuary, in the midst of cows, in the presence of Brahmins,
during Vedic recitation, and while eating, one should keep the right arm uncovered.
An upper garment must be worn during these five activities:
the private recitation of the Veda, the voiding of excrement, the giving of gifts, as well as eating and sipping water for purification. (39)

Sacrificial offerings, eating, giving, presenting oblations, and receiving gifts—these should not be performed with the hands outside the knees; the same rule is prescribed for sipping water (ācamana).
"All beings are supported by food; food is life," so says the Śruti.
Therefore, food must be given, for food is indeed the supreme oblation. (41)
"Sin is pacified by the oblation; the oblation is pacified by food;
food attains peace through the sacrificial fee—thus is our sacred tradition."
"‘He approaches,’ so we have heard. ||42||
Thus ends the sixth section in the second book of the Dharma-sūtra of Baudhāyana.
Thus ends the third chapter of the second book in the Dharma-sūtra of Baudhāyana.

Now, therefore, we shall explain the rule for the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*). (1) Having gone to a sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*), one who is already pure may or may not bathe; having washed his feet and hands and sipped water (*ācamana*), he should sprinkle himself with water that is fragrant, or with those [mantras] containing the word *abliṅga*, or with those addressed to Varuṇa, or with those of golden color, or with the *pāvamānī* verses, or with the *vyāhṛtis*, and with other purificatory texts (*pavitra*); thus he becomes pure. (2) Furthermore, they cite this: "Immersion in water is prescribed as a bath for all classes (*varṇa*);
however, for the twice-born (*dvijāti*), sprinkling accompanied by mantras is even more distinguished. (3)
And at the commencement of all ritual acts, before the time for the twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsana), one becomes pure by sprinkling oneself with this very collection of purifiers. ||4||

Moreover, they cite this: Sitting on *darbha* grass, holding *darbha* grass, with his hand containing water and facing westward, he should repeat the *Sāvitrī* one thousand times; or a hundred times by way of breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*); or ten times mentally, preceded and followed by the *praṇava* and accompanied by the seven *vyāhṛtis*; or, when exhausted, with three breath-controls, using the "Heart of Brahman" (*brahmahṛdaya*).

With two verses addressed to Varuṇa, he worships the night: "Hear this my call, O Varuṇa" and "That I implore of thee"—with these two. (9) In the same manner, standing in the morning facing the east, (10) with two verses addressed to Mitra, he worships the day: "Of Mitra, the supporter of the people" and "Mitra impels the folk"—with these two. (11)

Having begun even before sunrise, one may complete the morning recitation once the sun has risen; having begun before sunset, one may complete the evening recitation even well after [the sun has set]. ||12-13||
And for the sake of the continuity of both day and night, [one should perform this] during the two twilights when they are present. Furthermore, there are two verses sung by Prajāpati on this matter:
"Those Brahmins who do not attend upon the morning twilight that has not yet arrived, nor the evening twilight that has not yet passed—how can they be considered true Brahmins?"
"A righteous king may, at his pleasure, employ those Brahmins who do not constantly perform the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā) in the morning and evening for the labor of Śūdras. (15)

In that regard, if one transgresses in the evening, there is a fast for the night; if one transgresses in the morning, there is a fast for the day. (16) One obtains the fruit of standing and sitting. (17) Furthermore, they cite this: "Whatever sin has been committed with the sexual organ, or whatever has been done with the feet, or even with the arms, the mind, or speech—"
Having performed the evening twilight devotion, one is liberated from that by means of it. ||18||

He is joined with the night, and Varuṇa does not seize him. (19) Likewise, having performed the morning worship, he is released from the evil committed during the night. He is joined with the day, Mitra protects him, and Āditya leads him to the heavenly world. (21) Thus, worshipping day after day at the junctions of day and night, purified by the Veda, become one with the Veda, and following the sacred teaching, the Brāhmaṇa conquers the world of Brahman; so it is known. "He conquers the world of Brahman"—so it is known. (22)
Thus ends the seventh section in the second book of the Dharma-sūtra of Baudhāyana.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the second book of the Baudhāyana Dharmasūtra.

Then, having washed his hands and taken up his water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) and a lump of earth, he goes to a sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*) and washes his feet three times and himself three times. (1) Now, some say: "One must not enter a cremation ground, water, a temple, a cow-pen, or a place where there are Brahmins, without having first washed one's feet. (2) Then he approaches the water, saying: "I take refuge in Varuṇa, whose horns are of gold; grant me a way [into the water] when I have made my request.
Whatever I have eaten of the unrighteous, and whatever acceptance of gifts from the wicked [I have received]," (3)
Whatever evil I have done with my mind, speech, or action—may Indra, Varuṇa, Bṛhaspati, and Savitṛ purify that again and again. Thus [let it be]. (3)

Then he scoops up water with his joined palms, saying: "May the waters and plants be friendly to us. He sprinkles it toward that quarter in which direction he has someone whom he hates, saying: "May they be unfriendly to him who hates us and whom we hate."

Then, having touched water, he turns the water three times clockwise, saying: "Whatever in the waters is cruel, whatever is impure, whatever is unpeaceful—let that depart! (6) Having submerged himself in the water and emerged, (7) for one who remains in the water, no rinsing [of the mouth] is prescribed, nor the washing of clothes, nor the ritual touching of water. (8) If the waters should be obstructed, he worships them with this: "Homage to Agni accompanied by the waters; homage to Indra; homage to Varuṇa; homage to Vāruṇī; homage to the waters! (9)
Having crossed over and sipped water, once he has sipped, he should sip again:
"May the waters purify the earth; may the purified earth purify me.
May Brahmaṇaspati purify [me]; may the purified Veda purify me."
Whatever remains of food that is unfit to be eaten, or whatever evil deed I have committed—may the waters purify all of that in me, as well as the acceptance of gifts from the wicked; svāhā! ||10||

Having prepared the two strainers (*pavitre*), he purifies himself with water using the three verses beginning "O Waters, you are indeed the source of bliss" (*āpo hi ṣṭhā mayobhuvaḥ*), the four verses beginning "Golden-colored, pure, and purifying" (*hiraṇyavarṇāḥ śucayaḥ pāvakāḥ*), and the verse "The purifying one, belonging to the world of light" (*pavamānaḥ suvarjanaḥ*). Having purified himself with this section (*anuvāka*), he goes into the water, performs three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) while reciting the *Aghamarṣaṇa* hymn, and emerges. Having wrung out his garment, put on other unwashed clothes that have been washed and aired, and sipped water, he sits upon *darbha* grass, holding *darbha* blades, facing the east, and repeats the Sāvitrī verse a thousand times, or a hundred times, or an unlimited number of times, at least ten times.
Then he worships the sun with the verses: "Up from the darkness we [have risen]," "Up that one," "The bright one," "That eye established by the gods," and "He who has risen. (12)
Moreover, they also cite this: "The *praṇava*, the *vyāhṛtis*, and the *sāvitrī*—these five constitute the *brahmayajñas*; performed day after day, they purify the Brāhmaṇa from sin. (13)
Purified by the five Brahmayajñas, he thereafter satiates the deities. ||14||
Thus ends the eighth section in the second book of the Dharma Sūtra of Baudhāyana.

Om! Agni, Prajāpati, Soma, Rudra, Aditi, Bṛhaspati, and the Sarpas—these deities of the eastern doors, together with the constellations, the planets, the days and nights, and the muhūrtas, I satisfy. Om! And I satisfy the Vasus. 1.

Oṃ! I satiate the Pitṛs—Aryaman, Bhaga, Savitṛ, Tvaṣṭṛ, Vāyu, Indra, and Agni; these deities of the southern gate, together with the constellations, the planets, the days and nights, and the muhūrtas. Oṃ! And I satiate the Rudras. 2.

Oṃ, I satiate Mitra, Indra, the Great Ancestors, the Waters, the Viśvedevas, Brahmā, and Viṣṇu—these deities of the western doors, together with the constellations, the planets, the days and nights, and the muhūrtas. Oṃ, and I satiate the Ādityas as well. ||3||

Oṃ, I satiate the Vasus, Varuṇa, Aja Ekapād, Ahirbudhnya, Pūṣan, the two Aśvins, and Yama—these deities of the northern gate, together with the constellations, the planets, the days and nights, and the muhūrtas. Oṃ, I satiate the Viśvedevas. Oṃ, and I satiate the Sādhyas. 4.

Oṃ, I satiate Brahmā. Oṃ, I satiate Prajāpati. Oṃ, I satiate the Four-faced One. Oṃ, I satiate Parameṣṭhin. Oṃ, I satiate Hiraṇyagarbha. Oṃ, I satiate Svayaṃbhu. Oṃ, I satiate the attendants of Brahmā. Oṃ, I satiate the female attendants of Brahmā as well. Oṃ, I satiate Agni. Oṃ, I satiate Vāyu. Oṃ, I satiate Varuṇa. Oṃ, I satiate Sūrya. Oṃ, I satiate Candramas. Oṃ, I satiate the constellations. Oṃ, I satiate Sadyojāta. Oṃ, I satiate the Puruṣa of Bhūḥ. Oṃ, I satiate the Puruṣa of Bhuvaḥ. Oṃ, I satiate the Puruṣa of Suvaḥ. Oṃ, I satiate the Puruṣa of Bhūr-bhuvaḥ-suvaḥ. Oṃ, I satiate Bhūḥ. Oṃ, I satiate Bhuvaḥ. Oṃ, I satiate Suvaḥ. Oṃ, I satiate Mahas. Oṃ, I satiate Janaḥ. Oṃ, I satiate Tapaḥ. Oṃ, I satiate Satyam. ||5||

Oṃ, I satiate the god Bhava. Oṃ, I satiate the god Śarva. Oṃ, I satiate the god Īśāna. Oṃ, I satiate the god Paśupati. Oṃ, I satiate the god Rudra. Oṃ, I satiate the god Ugra. Oṃ, I satiate the god Bhīma. Oṃ, I satiate the god Mahān. Oṃ, I satiate the consort of the god Bhava. Oṃ, I satiate the consort of the god Śarva. Oṃ, I satiate the consort of the god Īśāna. Oṃ, I satiate the consort of the god Paśupati. Oṃ, I satiate the consort of the god Rudra. Oṃ, I satiate the consort of the god Ugra. Oṃ, I satiate the consort of the god Bhīma. Oṃ, I satiate the consort of the god Mahān. Oṃ, I satiate the son of the god Bhava. Oṃ, I satiate the son of the god Śarva. Oṃ, I satiate the son of the god Īśāna. Oṃ, I satiate the son of the god Paśupati. Oṃ, I satiate the son of the god Rudra. Oṃ, I satiate the son of the god Ugra. Oṃ, I satiate the son of the god Bhīma. Oṃ, I satiate the son of the god Mahān. Oṃ, I satiate the Rudras. Oṃ, I satiate the attendants of Rudra. Oṃ, I satiate the female attendants of Rudra as well. ||6||

Oṃ, I satiate Vighna. Oṃ, I satiate Vināyaka. Oṃ, I satiate Vīra. Oṃ, I satiate Sthūla. Oṃ, I satiate Varada. Oṃ, I satiate Hastimukha. Oṃ, I satiate Vakratuṇḍa. Oṃ, I satiate Ekadanta. Oṃ, I satiate Lambodara. Oṃ, I satiate the male attendants of Vighna. Oṃ, I satiate the female attendants of Vighna as well. (7)

Oṃ, I satiate Sanatkumāra. Oṃ, I satiate Skanda. Oṃ, I satiate Indra. Oṃ, I satiate Ṣaṣṭhī. Oṃ, I satiate Ṣaṇmukha. Oṃ, I satiate Jayanta. Oṃ, I satiate Viśākha. Oṃ, I satiate Mahāsena. Oṃ, I satiate Subrahmaṇya. Oṃ, I satiate the male attendants of Skanda. Oṃ, I satiate the female attendants of Skanda as well. ||8||

Oṃ, I satiate Āditya. Oṃ, I satiate Soma. Oṃ, I satiate Aṅgāraka. Oṃ, I satiate Budha. Oṃ, I satiate Bṛhaspati. Oṃ, I satiate Śukra. Oṃ, I satiate Śanaiścara. Oṃ, I satiate Rāhu. Oṃ, I satiate Ketu. ||9||

Oṃ, I satiate Keśava. Oṃ, I satiate Nārāyaṇa. Oṃ, I satiate Mādhava. Oṃ, I satiate Govinda. Oṃ, I satiate Viṣṇu. Oṃ, I satiate Madhusūdana. Oṃ, I satiate Trivikrama. Oṃ, I satiate Vāmana. Oṃ, I satiate Śrīdhara. Oṃ, I satiate Hṛṣīkeśa. Oṃ, I satiate Padmanābha. Oṃ, I satiate Dāmodara. Oṃ, I satiate the goddess Śrī. Oṃ, I satiate the goddess Sarasvatī. Oṃ, I satiate Puṣṭi. Oṃ, I satiate Tuṣṭi. Oṃ, I satiate Garuḍa. Oṃ, I satiate the attendants of Viṣṇu. Oṃ, I satiate the female attendants of Viṣṇu. ||10||

Oṃ, I satiate Yama. Oṃ, I satiate Yamarāja. Oṃ, I satiate Dharma. Oṃ, I satiate Dharmarāja. Oṃ, I satiate Kāla. Oṃ, I satiate Nīla. Oṃ, I satiate Mṛtyu. Oṃ, I satiate Vaivasvata. Oṃ, I satiate Citra. Oṃ, I satiate Citragupta. Oṃ, I satiate Audumbara. Oṃ, I satiate the male attendants of Vaivasvata. Oṃ, I satiate the female attendants of Vaivasvata as well. ||11||

Oṃ, I satiate the gods of the earth. Oṃ, I satiate Kāśyapa. Oṃ, I satiate the intermediate space. Oṃ, I satiate Knowledge. Oṃ, I satiate Dhanvantari. Oṃ, I satiate the attendants of Dhanvantari. Oṃ, I satiate the female attendants of Dhanvantari as well. ||12||
Now, [the rule for] the nivīta [manner of wearing the sacred thread]. ||13||

Oṃ, I satiate the ṛṣis. Oṃ, I satiate the great ṛṣis (maharṣis). Oṃ, I satiate the supreme ṛṣis (paramarṣis). Oṃ, I satiate the brahmin-ṛṣis (brahmarṣis). Oṃ, I satiate the divine ṛṣis (devarṣis). Oṃ, I satiate the royal ṛṣis (rājarṣis). Oṃ, I satiate the learned ṛṣis (śrutarṣis). Oṃ, I satiate the people-ṛṣis (janarṣis). Oṃ, I satiate the ascetic ṛṣis (taparṣis). Oṃ, I satiate the truthful ṛṣis (satyarṣis). Oṃ, I satiate the seven ṛṣis (saptarṣis). Oṃ, I satiate the section-ṛṣis (kāṇḍarṣis). Oṃ, I satiate the female ṛṣis (ṛṣikās). Oṃ, I satiate the wives of the ṛṣis (ṛṣipatnīs). Oṃ, I satiate the sons of the ṛṣis (ṛṣiputrās). Oṃ, I satiate the grandsons of the ṛṣis (ṛṣipautrās).

Oṃ, I satiate Kāṇva Baudhāyana. Oṃ, I satiate Āpastamba, the author of the Sūtras. Oṃ, I satiate Satyāṣāḍha Hiraṇyakeśin. Oṃ, I satiate Yājñavalkya, the Vājasaneyin. Oṃ, I satiate Āśvalāyana Śaunaka. Oṃ, I satiate Vyāsa. Oṃ, I satiate Vasiṣṭha.

Oṃ, I satiate the Praṇava. Oṃ, I satiate the Vyāhṛtis. Oṃ, I satiate Sāvitrī. Oṃ, I satiate Gāyatrī. Oṃ, I satiate the Metres (Chandas). Oṃ, I satiate the Ṛgveda. Oṃ, I satiate the Yajurveda. Oṃ, I satiate the Sāmaveda. Oṃ, I satiate the Atharvaveda. Oṃ, I satiate the Atharvāṅgirases. Oṃ, I satiate the Itihāsas and Purāṇas. Oṃ, I satiate all the Vedas. Oṃ, I satiate all the divine beings. Oṃ, I satiate all living beings. Thus [it is said]. 14.
Thus ends the ninth section in the second book of the Dharma-sūtra of Baudhāyana.
Then, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī).

Oṃ, I satiate the fathers with *svadhā* and salutation. Oṃ, I satiate the grandfathers with *svadhā* and salutation. Oṃ, I satiate the great-grandfathers with *svadhā* and salutation. Oṃ, I satiate the mothers with *svadhā* and salutation. Oṃ, I satiate the grandmothers with *svadhā* and salutation. Oṃ, I satiate the great-grandmothers with *svadhā* and salutation. Oṃ, I satiate the maternal grandfathers with *svadhā* and salutation. Oṃ, I satiate the maternal grandfathers’ fathers with *svadhā* and salutation. Oṃ, I satiate the maternal grandfathers’ great-grandfathers with *svadhā* and salutation. Oṃ, I satiate the maternal grandmothers with *svadhā* and salutation. Oṃ, I satiate the maternal grandfathers’ mothers with *svadhā* and salutation. Oṃ, I satiate the maternal grandfathers’ great-grandmothers with *svadhā* and salutation. ||1||

Om, I satiate the teachers with *svadhā* and salutation. Om, I satiate the wives of the teachers with *svadhā* and salutation. Om, I satiate the gurus with *svadhā* and salutation. Om, I satiate the wives of the gurus with *svadhā* and salutation. Om, I satiate the friends with *svadhā* and salutation. Om, I satiate the wives of the friends with *svadhā* and salutation. Om, I satiate the kinsmen with *svadhā* and salutation. Om, I satiate the wives of the kinsmen with *svadhā* and salutation. Om, I satiate the ministers with *svadhā* and salutation. Om, I satiate the wives of the ministers with *svadhā* and salutation. Om, I satiate all [male relatives] with *svadhā* and salutation. Om, I satiate all [female relatives] with *svadhā* and salutation. Thus [it is said]. 2.

At every sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*), he pours out water, saying: "Carrying strength, nectar, ghee, milk, ambrosia, and flowing liquor—you are the *svadhā* offering; satisfy my ancestors! Be satisfied, be satisfied, be satisfied! (TS 1.8.5.1–2)

One should not perform rites for the gods while wearing only a single garment or while one's clothes are wet; some say this also applies to rites connected with the ancestors. Some say this also applies to rites connected with the ancestors.
Thus ends the tenth section in the second book of the Baudhāyana Dharmasūtra.
Thus ends the fifth chapter of the second book in the Dharma-sūtra of Baudhāyana.

Now, there are these five great sacrifices; they are indeed the great sacrificial sessions: the sacrifice to the gods, the sacrifice to the ancestors, the sacrifice to the spirits, the sacrifice to men, and the sacrifice to Brahman. ||1||
Day after day he should offer with the word *svāhā* until the wood is consumed; in this way, he completes this sacrifice to the gods. ||2||
Day by day, one should offer the *svadhā* oblation, even if it is only from a vessel of water; in this way, one completes this sacrifice to the ancestors (*pitṛyajña*). ||3||
Day after day he should pay homage as far as the flowers; in this way, he completes this sacrifice to beings (bhūtayajña). ||4||
Day after day, one should give food to Brahmins, even down to roots, fruits, and vegetables; in this way, one fulfills this sacrifice to men. ||5||

Day by day one should perform the private recitation (*svādhyāya*) at least as far as the syllable *oṃ*. In this way, one completes this sacrifice to Brahman (*brahmayajña*). Indeed, the private recitation is the sacrifice to Brahman. Of this very sacrifice to Brahman, speech is the *juhū* ladle, the mind the *upabhṛt*, the eye the *dhruvā*, intelligence the *sruva* spoon, truth the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*), and the heavenly world the conclusion. As great a world as one wins by giving away this earth filled with wealth, so great a world does one win—and even more, an inexhaustible one—who, knowing this, studies his private recitation. He conquers rebirth. Therefore, the private recitation must be studied; for thus says the Brāhmaṇa.
Moreover, they also cite this: "If one, well-anointed, well-fed, and lying on a comfortable bed, studies any particular sacrifice, by that very sacrifice he has sacrificed. (8)

Regarding this very Dharma, some say that its division is fourfold because it has not been seen [in its entirety]. Those who say "there are four" are proponents of ritual action (*karmavāda*). These four consist of the *iṣṭi*-sacrifices, the animal sacrifices (*pāśuka*), the *saumika* (Soma) sacrifices, and the wood-offering oblations (*dārvihoma*).
Concerning this,
the following verse declares: "The four paths leading to the gods which extend between heaven and earth..."
"O gods, entrust them all here to him among you who shall bring about non-defeat and non-decay. ||11||
The student, the householder, the forest-dweller, and the wandering mendicant. ||12||
A student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī) shall serve his teacher until death. ||13||

The forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) follows the traditional conduct prescribed in the *Vaikhānasa* scriptures. A *vaikhānasa* dwells in the forest, subsisting on roots and fruits, devoted to austerity, performing ablutions at the three daily libations, maintaining the sacred fire according to the *Śrāmaṇaka* rite, eating only non-village-grown food, and honoring the gods, ancestors, spirits, men, and sages. He is hospitable to all guests; he may consume even meat that is not forbidden, provided it is obtained by purchase. He must not stand upon land ploughed by a plow, nor enter a village. Wearing matted hair and clothed in bark or skins, he should not eat more than once a year.

A wandering mendicant, having abandoned his kinsmen and remaining without possessions, should go forth according to the prescribed rule. (16) Having gone to the forest. (17) With his topknot shaven. (18) Clothed in a loincloth. (19) Staying in one place during the rainy season. (20) Wearing saffron-colored robes. (21)

He should beg for alms when the pestle has been laid down, when the embers have been extinguished, and when the exchange of bowls has ceased. (22) He should not harbor malice toward living beings through the restraints of speech, mind, and action. (23) He should carry a purifier for the sake of purification. (24) He should perform all water-related rites with water that has been drawn up and strained. (25) Having cast aside Vedic rituals, they say, "Severed from both ends, let us cling to the middle state. (26)
But the teachers maintain that there is only one stage of life, because the others do not result in procreation.

Regarding this, they cite an example: There was indeed an Asura named Kapila, the son of Prahlāda. Competing with the gods, he created these various distinctions. A wise person should not respect them. (28)

Because they have not been seen [in the texts]. "Those which are fourfold" refers to the discourse on ritual action (*karmavāda*) concerning the *iṣṭi*, *paśu*, *saumika*, and *dārvihoma* sacrifices. (29)
Regarding this, the following verse is recited:
"This is the eternal greatness of a Brahmin; he does not increase by action, nor does he become less."
Having known the path and the state of that very Self, one is not smeared by evil action. ||30||
He should say:
"By that splendor kindled by which the sun shines,
may the father, possessed of his son, [be united] with his son in womb after womb."
One who does not know the Veda does not truly perceive that great Self, the experiencer of all, which is the ultimate goal. ||31||
These who move neither hither nor thither—
neither Brahmins nor those who pour the libation—
they have resorted to speech with evil intent.
"They spread out their thread [of sacrifice], not knowing [the end]," so it is said. ||32||

"O Agni, through offspring may I attain immortality. Indeed, when being born, a Brāhmaṇa is born with three debts: he owes the sages the debt of studentship (*brahmacarya*), the gods the debt of sacrifice (*yajña*), and the ancestors the debt of offspring (*prajā*). In this way, there are innumerable statements concerning the connection with these debts. (33)
The threefold knowledge, the life of celibate studentship, procreation, faith, austerity, sacrifice, and the giving of gifts—
those who perform these, with them indeed do we abide.
"Having become dust, he perishes while praising another;
he perishes while praising another.
||34|| Thus ends the eleventh section in the second book of the *Baudhāyana-dharmasūtra*.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the second book of the *Dharmasūtra* of Baudhāyana.
Now we shall explain the oblations to the vital breaths (prāṇāhuti) of those who are modest, of the Yāyāvara class, and who sacrifice to the Self.

At the conclusion of all necessary duties, having sat down facing the east in a place that has been swept and smeared with cow-dung, he should, upon seeing that food being brought, perform the ritual salutation with the words: *bhūr bhuvaḥ suvar oṃ*. Having performed this salutation, he should restrain his speech. He should sprinkle water clockwise around the placed food with the Great Utterances (*mahāvyāhṛtis*), while not releasing it from his left hand. Having first drunk water with the formula, "Thou art the under-layer for immortality" (*amṛtopastaraṇam asi*), he offers the oblations to the vital breaths (*prāṇāhutis*) with the food.

Seated in the out-breath (*prāṇa*), I offer the nectar; may the auspicious one enter me for the sake of non-burning. *Svāhā* to the out-breath! Seated in the in-breath (*apāna*), I offer the nectar; may the auspicious one enter me for the sake of non-burning. *Svāhā* to the in-breath! Seated in the diffused breath (*vyāna*), I offer the nectar; may the auspicious one enter me for the sake of non-burning. *Svāhā* to the diffused breath! Seated in the upward breath (*udāna*), I offer the nectar; may the auspicious one enter me for the sake of non-burning. *Svāhā* to the upward breath! Seated in the equalizing breath (*samāna*), I offer the nectar; may the auspicious one enter me for the sake of non-burning. *Svāhā* to the equalizing breath! Thus [ends the third section].

Having offered five oblations of food to the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), he should eat further in silence, meditating mentally on Prajāpati; he should not release speech in the interval. If he should release speech in the interval, having muttered "bhūr bhuvaḥ suvar oṃ," he should eat again.

Having seen skin, hair, nails, insects, or mouse-droppings in that place, one should remove the food-ball (*piṇḍa*), sprinkle it with water, scatter ashes over it, sprinkle it again with water, and then consume it after it has been verbally consecrated as pure. Furthermore, they cite this:

"Sitting down, facing the east, with speech controlled, one should eat the food without disparaging it; without letting it spill, and with the mind fixed on it, having eaten, one should touch fire and water."
One should not bite with the teeth any food, cakes, bulbs, roots, fruits, or meat. (8) One should not eat until completely satiated. (9)

"Thou art the covering of immortality. Having drunk water from above and sipped [water for purification], he touches the region of his heart, saying: "Thou art the knot of the vital breaths; enter me as Rudra the destroyer; swell with this food. (10)
Having sipped water again, he lets the water flow from his hands over his right big toe, [reciting]:
"The Person the size of a thumb resides within the thumb;
the Lord of the entire world, the Master, the consumer of all, is pleased. (11)

With hands raised, one should perform the consecration of the oblation (*hutānumantraṇa*): "Having entered into faith, the immortal oblation has been offered into the *prāṇa*. Satisfy the *prāṇa* with food. Having entered into faith, the immortal oblation has been offered into the *apāna*. Satisfy the *apāna* with food. Having entered into faith, the immortal oblation has been offered into the *vyāna*. Satisfy the *vyāna* with food. Having entered into faith, the immortal oblation has been offered into the *udāna*. Satisfy the *udāna* with food. Having entered into faith, the immortal oblation has been offered into the *samāna*. Satisfy the *samāna* with food. [These are] the five [verses]. 12.
"May my self [be united] with Brahman for the sake of immortality. ||13|| And one should unite the self with the Imperishable (akṣara). ||14||
Among those who perform all types of sacrifices, the one who sacrifices to the Self is distinguished. Furthermore, they cite this: [16]
Thus ends the twelfth section in the second book of the Baudhāyana Dharmasūtra.
For just as a tuft of reed-wool, when cast into a fire, is consumed by flame, even so are all the sins of one who sacrifices to the Self utterly burnt away. (1)
He who eats alone becomes the possessor of sin alone;
the thoughtless man obtains food in vain. ||2||
He should offer oblations in this very manner every day, both evening and morning; or he may do so with water alone in the evening.
Moreover, they cite this example:
"One should feed the guests first, and immediately thereafter those who are pregnant,
as well as children, the elderly, the destitute, and especially the sick."
But he who eats before these [deities] according to the rule, not knowing that he himself is being consumed, does not eat; rather, he is eaten. (5)
"Restraining his speech, he should eat the remains of the food after [satisfying] the ancestors, the deities, his servants, as well as his mother, father, and teacher; thus is dharma ordained. (6)
Moreover, they also cite this:
"An ascetic should eat eight morsels, a forest-dweller sixteen, a householder thirty-two, and for a student there is no fixed limit. (7)
"The maintainer of the sacred fires, the ox, and the student—these three achieve perfection only while eating; for them, there is no perfection for those who do not eat. ||8||
Whether he be a householder or a student, if one performs penance while fasting, he becomes an outcast by violating the *prāṇāgnihotra*. (9)
Except in the case of penance; for penance, that very same rule applies. Furthermore, they cite this:
"He who never eats between his morning meal and his evening meal is always one who observes a fast. (10–11)
When food is withheld, one should recite the *prāṇāgnihotra* mantras;
and when sacrificial materials are unavailable, one should recite the *tretāgnihotra* mantras. ||12||
Practicing in this way, one is fit for becoming Brahman; "one is fit for becoming Brahman"—thus [it is said]. ||13||
Thus ends the thirteenth section in the second book of the *Dharmasūtra* of Baudhāyana.
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the second book of the Dharma-sūtra of Baudhāyana.
It pertains to the ancestors, bestows long life, leads to heaven, brings fame, and is a rite for nourishment. ||1||

One who has mastered the *trimadhu*, the *triṇāciketa*, and the *trisuparṇa*; one who maintains the five fires; one learned in the six auxiliary sciences (*ṣaḍaṅga*); one who knows the *śīrṣaka*; one who chants the *jyeṣṭhasāman*; and a *snātaka*—these are the sanctifiers of the row (*paṅktipāvana*). In their absence, one who knows the secret doctrines (*rahasyavid*) [may be invited]. The greatness of the *śrāddha* consists in the *ṛc*s, the *yajus*s, and the *sāman*s; therefore, one should feed even a *sapiṇḍa* relative who possesses such knowledge.

He should softly recite, with the intention of purifying the mind, the *Sāman* chants that destroy demons, the *Yajus* formulas endowed with self-power (*svadhā*), the honey-verses (*madhūrcas*), and the purificatory texts (*pavitrāṇi*).

On the previous day, or at dawn on that very day, he should invite at least three, an odd number of pure men who possess good conduct, are learned in the Vedas, are not related by birth, lineage, or mantra, and are conversant with the sacred texts; having invited them, he causes them to sit facing either east or north upon seats prepared with Darbha grass.

Then, having caused them to receive water mixed with sesame seeds and having adorned them with perfumes and garlands, he says, "I shall perform the offering in the fire. Being permitted, he prepares the fire, strews grass around it, performs the preliminary rites up to the *agnimukha*, and offers three oblations of food alone:
"To Soma, drunk by the ancestors, *svadhā*! Adoration! *Svāhā*!
"To Yama, accompanied by the Aṅgirases and the ancestors, *svadhā*! Adoration! *Svāhā*!"
To Agni Kavyavāhana Sviṣṭakṛt, svadhā! Homage! Svāhā! ||7||
Having sprinkled the food with the remainder of that [ghee], he should offer these same three oblations of the food. ||8||
One should offer a ball of food for birds. For it is known from scripture that "the ancestors move about in the form of birds."
Then he touches the other [parts] with his hand, including the thumb. ||11||

"Earth is the rim of your [vessel]; fire is your overseer; your greatness is for the non-neglect of what has been given. Earth is your vessel, heaven is the lid. I offer you into the mouth of Brahman; I offer you into the out-breath and in-breath of the learned Brahmins. You are imperishable; may you not perish among the ancestors there in yonder world."

“Vāyu is the listener for you who are equal to the intermediate space; the *yajus* formulas are your greatness for the non-neglect of what has been given. The earth is your vessel, the sky is the lid. I offer you into the mouth of Brahman; I offer you into the out-breath and in-breath of the learned Brahmins. You are imperishable; may you not perish among the grandfathers there in that world.”

The sun is your announcer, O Dyusamanta; the Sāmans are the greatness given to you for the sake of non-negligence. The earth is your vessel, the sky your lid. I offer you into the mouth of the Brahman; I offer you into the out-breath and in-breath of the learned Brāhmaṇas. You are imperishable; may you not perish among my great-grandfathers there in yonder world. ||12||
Thus ends the fourteenth section in the second book of the Dharma-sūtra of Baudhāyana.
Now, indeed, it is said: ||1||
One should sprinkle that food with the remnants from the *agnaukaraṇa* offering;
for that which is given without the thumb does not indeed gratify the ancestors. ||2||
Food offered to the ancestors is presented, released from both branches;
in that interval, the evil-minded Asuras wait in ambush. (3)
Yātudhānas and piśācas plunder that sacrificial offering;
likewise, when sesame seeds are given, the asuras who are not entitled to them [plunder it] under the power of anger.
If one who wears saffron robes performs recitations, fire-oblations, or accepts gifts, that oblation—whether for the gods or the ancestors—does not reach its divine destination. (5)
That which is given without the thumb, that which is accepted in the same manner, and he who sips water while standing—by such acts, one does not attain prosperity. ||6||

The offering of water at the beginning and at the end applies everywhere. (7) From the *jaya* oblation onwards, it is according to the prescribed rule. (8) The remainder has been stated in the context of the *aṣṭakā* fire-oblation. (9)
One should feed two at a rite for the gods and three at a rite for the ancestors, or one for each of the two; even if very wealthy, one should not indulge in excessive elaboration.
Excessive elaboration destroys these five: hospitality, proper time and place, purity, and the excellence of the Brahmins; therefore, one should avoid it.
From his chest come the fathers, from his left side the grandfathers, from his right side the great-grandfathers, and from his back the seekers of the funeral cakes. ||12||
Thus ends the fifteenth section in the second book of the *Dharmasūtra* of Baudhāyana.
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the second book of the Dharma-sūtra of Baudhāyana.
1. This is the instruction for one desiring offspring. 2. "The designation is based on the cause of procreation," so said the two Aśvins.
Endowed with long life and austerity, devoted to Vedic study and sacrifice, and having conquered his senses, he should diligently procreate offspring within his own respective caste. (3)
From birth, a Brahmin enters into three debts;
by discharging them, he becomes self-possessed and liberated from doubt regarding dharma. ||4||
Having honored the seers through Vedic study, Indra with the Soma sacrifice, and his ancestors with progeny, he becomes free from debt and rejoices in heaven. (5)
Through a son one conquers the worlds; through a grandson one attains immortality;
and through a great-grandson one ascends to heaven itself. ||6||

And it is known from scripture: "A Brāhmaṇa, being born, is indeed born with three debts—to the sages through studentship, to the gods through sacrifice, and to the ancestors through progeny. Thus the Veda demonstrates this connection with debts. (7)
By producing a virtuous son, one delivers oneself. ||8||
By obtaining a virtuous son, one rescues seven descendants, seven ancestors, six others, and oneself— the seventh— from sin and from fear.
Therefore, having produced offspring, one attains the fruit. (10) Therefore, one should diligently produce offspring. (11) By means of the application of medicinal herbs and mantras. (12)
The instruction regarding that [knowledge] is taught by way of a commonality of scriptural tradition: "Because it bears fruit for all castes. Because it bears fruit. ||13–14||
Thus ends the sixteenth section in the second book of the Dharma-sūtra of Baudhāyana.
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the second book of the Baudhāyana Dharmasūtra.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the procedure for renunciation. ||1||

Therefore, according to some, one who is already a practitioner of celibacy (brahmacaryavān) may go forth as a wanderer. Now, [this applies] to those of the Śālīna and Yāyāvara classes who are childless; or to one whose family line has failed, or who, having established his offspring in their own duties, [does so]; they prescribe renunciation (saṃnyāsa) after the age of seventy; or for a forest-dweller (vānaprastha) upon the cessation of ritual action.
This is the eternal greatness of a Brahmin: he does not increase by action, nor does he become less.
Having realized the path and found that very Self, he is not sullied by evil action.
One is not smeared by evil karma. ||7||
He is eternal because he leads one to the state of no further rebirth. He is greatness because he causes one to attain the Great.

Having shaved his hair, beard, body hair, and nails, he prepares: staffs, a sling, a water-purifier, a water-pot, and a bowl (10–11). Having taken these, at the edge of the village or the boundary of the village, or in a fire-hut, having consumed the threefold mixture of clarified butter, milk, and curds, he shall fast (12); or [he may consume] water (13).
Oṃ bhūḥ, I enter the Sāvitrī: "That excellent splendor of Savitṛ. Oṃ bhuvaḥ, I enter the Sāvitrī: "We meditate upon the glory of the divine.
Oṃ suvaḥ, I enter the Sāvitrī: "Who may impel our thoughts. Thus [three times].
Then [he recites] by half-verses in reverse order, and then both together and separately. ||14||
It is known from scripture that by leading oneself from one stage of life (āśrama) to the next, one becomes purified by Brahman. Furthermore, they cite this:
"Having gone from stage to stage, having offered oblations with the fire-sacrifice, and having become exhausted by alms and offerings, one finally becomes a mendicant."
This very monk [strives] for the infinite. ||17||

Before sunset, having kindled the *gārhapatya* fire, brought the *anvāhāryapacana* fire, and drawn out the flaming *āhavanīya* fire, he melts clarified butter over the *gārhapatya*, purifies it, takes four portions into the *sruva*-ladle, and offers a full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) into the *āhavanīya* while it contains a fuel-stick, saying: "Oṃ svāhā! This is known as the "preparation of the sacred fires" (*brahmānvādhāna*).

Then, when the evening agnihotra has been offered, having spread grass to the north of the gārhapatya fire and placed the vessels upon it in pairs with their openings facing downwards, and having spread darbha grass in the seat of the Brahman to the south of the āhavanīya fire and laid a black antelope skin over it, he remains awake for that night.
A Brahmin who, knowing this, fasts during the night of Brahmā, consigns his fires within himself, and dies, overcomes all evil; he overcomes even the murder of a Brahmin.

Then, having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, he performs the morning *agnihotra* at the proper time. Then, having strewn the *pṛṣṭhyā* line and having carried forward the water, he offers a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara. That well-known sacrifice is completed.

He throws the Agnihotra vessels—those not made of clay and not made of stone—into the Āhavanīya fire. He throws the two kindling woods (araṇī) into the Gārhapatya fire with the mantra: "May you two be of one mind for us. He consigns the fires into himself, and he smells each one of them three times with the mantra: "O Agni, that body of yours which is fit for sacrifice..."

Then, standing within the sacrificial altar (antarvedi), he recites three times in a low voice and three times aloud: “*Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ; renounced by me, renounced by me, renounced by me.*” For it is known from scripture: “The gods are indeed true to their word thrice. He then pours out a full handful of water, saying: “Fearlessness to all beings from me. Furthermore, they cite this:
“When a sage wanders about after having granted fearlessness to all beings, no fear arises for him from any being, even in this world.”
He remains restrained in speech. ||31||

"May my friend protect [me]," with these words he takes up the staff. (32) "Whatever is on the further shore of this mist," with these words he takes hold of the sling. (33) "With that purifier by which the gods [crossed over]," with these words he takes the water-purifier. (34) "With that light by which the gods rose upward," with these words he takes the water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*). (35) With the seven *vyāhṛtis*, he takes the vessel. (36)

Having taken up his staff, a sling, a water-strainer, a water-pot, and a bowl, he goes to where there is water; having bathed, sipped water, and purified himself with the *surabhimatī*, *ābliṅga*, *vāruṇī*, *hiraṇyavarṇā*, and *pāvamānī* verses, he enters the water and performs sixteen breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) while reciting the *aghamarṣaṇa* hymn; then, having emerged, wrung out his garment, put on another clean garment, and sipped water.

"Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ. Having taken up the water-purifier, he offers libations: "Oṃ bhūḥ, I satisfy; Oṃ bhuvaḥ, I satisfy; Oṃ suvaḥ, I satisfy; Oṃ mahaḥ, I satisfy; Oṃ janaḥ, I satisfy; Oṃ tapaḥ, I satisfy; Oṃ satyam, I satisfy. (37)
Having offered a reverential salutation with joined palms to the ancestors as to the gods, [he says]: "Oṃ bhūḥ svadhā; Oṃ bhuvaḥ svadhā; Oṃ suvaḥ svadhā; Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ suvar mahar namaḥ. ||38||
Then, with the two [verses] "ud u tyam" and "citram," he worships the Āditya.

"Om"—this is Brahman. Indeed, this light that shines yonder is Brahman; this light that shines yonder is the Veda; this light that shines yonder is that which is to be known. Thus does he satisfy himself; thus does he pay homage to the Self. The Self is Brahman; the Self is the light. (40) One should repeat the Sāvitrī one thousand times, or one hundred times, or an unlimited number of times. (41)

Saying "Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ suvar," he takes up a water-purifier and draws water. (42) From this point forward, one should not sip water that has not been drawn out, nor that which is unstrained, nor that which is unpurified. (43)
And from this point onward, he shall not wear white clothing. ||44||
Thus ends the seventeenth section in the second book of the *Dharmasūtra* of Baudhāyana.
He may be either a single-staffed ascetic (*ekadaṇḍī*) or a triple-staffed ascetic (*tridaṇḍī*). Now, these are the vows:

non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, and the avoidance of sexual intercourse; as well as renunciation. There are exactly five secondary vows (*upavrata*): freedom from anger, service to the teacher, vigilance, purity, and purity of food.

Now follows the practice of begging for alms. When the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice has been concluded, he should seek alms from Brāhmaṇas who are *śālīna* or *yāyāvara*. He should prompt [the host] with the word "bhavat" (sir) placed first. He should wait for as long as it takes to milk a cow.

Then, having returned from the practice of begging for alms, having set down his hands and feet in a clean place and washed them, he should offer [the food] before the sun with the hymns "Upa tyaṃ jātavedasam" and "Citram". He offers it to Brahman with the hymn "Brahma jajñānam". ||7||

It is known: from the time of the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*) onwards, the fires belong to the sacrificer alone. His out-breath (*prāṇa*) is the *gārhapatya* fire; his in-breath (*apāna*) is the *anvāhāryapacana*; his diffused breath (*vyāna*) is the *āhavanīya*; and his upward-breath (*udāna*) and equalizing breath (*samāna*) are the *sabhya* and *āvasathya* fires. These five fires are established within the self; he offers oblations into the self alone. (8)
It is known that this very person is a sacrifice to the Self, established in the Self, grounded in the Self, and leads the Self to security. ||9||

Having first shared [the food] with living beings out of compassion, he should touch the remainder with water and eat it like medicine. (10) Having eaten and sipped water, he worships the sun with the "Luminous" verse: "Up from the darkness we... and after muttering: "May speech be in my mouth; may breath be in my nostrils. (11)
One should eat only as much food as is necessary for the maintenance of life—food that is unasked for, not prepared in anticipation, and obtained by chance. ||12||
Moreover, they cite this example:
"An ascetic should eat eight morsels, a forest-dweller sixteen, a householder thirty-two, and a student an unlimited amount. (13)

He may beg alms from members of all castes, or he may eat food from a single person among the twice-born; or alternatively, he may beg from members of all castes, provided that he does not eat food from a single person among the twice-born. (14)

Now, regarding that which the teachers declare as the Upaniṣad, they cite this: for one who is engaged in the vows of standing, silence, the hero’s posture (vīrāsana), bathing at the three libations (savana), touching water, and observing the fasts on the fourth, sixth, and eighth lunar days, there is the practice of subsisting on grains, oil-cakes, barley-gruel, curd, and milk. ||15||

In that regard, one engaged in silence (*mauna*) should—whether with elders learned in the three Vedas, teachers, sages, or others belonging to the stages of life (*āśrama*) who are deeply versed in scripture—keep his teeth joined to his teeth, facing inward, and speak only as much as is necessary for a purpose. It is known from scripture: "He should not speak with women, nor where there would be a transgression. (16) There should be practice of any one of these: a fixed posture (*sthāna*), silence (*mauna*), or the hero’s posture (*vīrāsana*). One should not bring these three together. (17) Wherever he goes, he should observe only so much [of the vow] as is possible; it is known from scripture that in times of distress, there should be no transgression. (18)

For one who is devoted to the vows of standing, silence, the heroic posture, bathing at the three libations, and sipping water at the fourth, sixth, and eighth periods of the day, there are eight things that do not destroy the merit of his vows: water, roots, ghee, milk, sacrificial oblation, the desire of a Brahmin, the word of a teacher, and medicine. (19)

He should mutter the Agnihotra mantras at evening and at dawn. Having performed the evening twilight worship with the Vāruṇī verses, he should perform the morning twilight worship with the Maitrī verses.

"Let him be without fire, without a fixed dwelling, without shelter, and without refuge; let the sage seek the village only for the sake of alms, and let him abandon speech during his private Vedic recitation. (22)

And it is known: "The Ṛg-verses are limited, the Sāman-chants are limited, the Yajus-formulas are limited; but of this Brahman there is no end. One should explain that to the one who responds: "That is the response (pratigara). ||23||

In this very way, until the liberation from the body, he is a tree-root-dweller who has renounced the Veda. The Veda is a tree; its root is the *praṇava*. The Veda consists of the *praṇava*. Meditating upon the *praṇava*, one who possesses the *praṇava* becomes fit for union with Brahman; so said Prajāpati.
One should wash the vessel for the Brahman with the seven *vyāhṛtis*. "One should wash"—thus [it is said]. 27.
Thus ends the eighteenth section in the second book of the Dharma-sūtra of Baudhāyana.
Thus ends the tenth chapter of the second book in the Dharma-sūtra of Baudhāyana.
Thus ends the second question.

Now, for those who desire the Dharma and subsist by the nine modes of livelihood—namely, the Śālīnas, the Yāyāvaras, and the Cakracaras—the term "vṛtti" (mode of livelihood) is used because they subsist by means of them. ||1-2||

Because of their dependence on a hall (for shelter), they are called *śālīna*. Because they travel with excellent means of subsistence, they are called *yāyāvara*. Because they move in a circular sequence, they are called *cakracara*.

We shall explain them in detail. (6) These nine modes of livelihood are: the sixfold abstaining (*ṣaṇṇivartanī*), the spade-method (*kauddālī*), the constant (*dhruvā*), the washing-method (*saṃprakṣālanī*), the gathering (*samūhā*), the plowing-method (*phālanī*), the gleaning of ears and grains (*śiloñchā*), the pigeon-method (*kāpotā*), and the successful-wish-method (*siddhecchā*). (7) Or rather, there is yet another tenth mode of livelihood for these very [nine]. (8)

Until the completion of the nine-day period, he has his hair, beard, body hair, and nails shaved off and prepares [the following]: a black antelope skin, a water-pot, a staff, a shoulder-bag, and a woolen garment with a fringe. Having performed either the Traidhātavīya sacrifice or the Vaiśvānarī sacrifice, he shall set out.

Then, in the morning when the sun has risen, having kindled the fires according to the sūtra, having melted the clarified butter over the *gārhapatya* fire and purified it, having heated and wiped the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, and having taken four portions of butter into the *sruk*, he offers the oblation to Vāstoṣpati in the *āhavanīya* fire. Having recited the invitatory verse (*puronuvākyā*): "O Vāstoṣpati, acknowledge us," he offers with the offering verse (*yājyā*): "O Vāstoṣpati, with your auspicious assembly... (VS 7.54). ||13-14||
Some say that everyone who has established the sacred fires [is eligible]. Others say that only the Yāyāvara [is eligible].
Having gone out, he stays at the edge of the village or at the boundary of the village; there he builds a hut or a monastery, or he enters one already built. ||17||
Whatever purpose each of the prepared items, such as the black antelope skin and others, serves, one should employ them for that respective purpose. ||18||

The attendance upon the sacred fires is well known; the performance of the New and Full Moon sacrifices is well known; the practice of the five great sacrifices is well known. The threshing of the produced grains is observed [as follows]: either with the formula "I thresh what is pleasing to all the gods," or silently; having prepared them, he completes the task. 20.
For him, teaching, officiating at sacrifices, and accepting gifts cease, as do all other sacrificial rites. ||21||

And it is observed that the sacrificial oblation (*haviṣya*) to be used for undertaking the vow (*vratopāyanīya*) consists of the following: namely, mixed with clarified butter, mixed with curd, free from pungent salt, without meat, and not stale. ||22–23||

He observes celibacy, or he approaches his wife only during her season. ||24|| On every sacred day (parvan), there shall be the shaving of hair, beard, body hair, and nails, as well as the rules for purification. ||25|| Now they also quote: "It is heard that purification is of two kinds, which has been practiced by the learned:
external purification is freedom from stains and odors; internal purification is non-violence. ||26||
The limbs are purified by water; the intellect is purified by knowledge;
the elemental self (bhūtātman) is purified by non-violence; and the mind is purified by truth. ||27||
Thus ends the first chapter of the third book in the Dharma-sūtra of Baudhāyana.

Regarding this term *ṣaṇṇivartanī*: [it refers to] one who performs exactly six furrows (*nivartanāni*) without causing injury. He sets aside a portion for the owner, or he takes it with the owner’s permission. Before breakfast, he should be a ploughman, with his nostrils unsewn and his testicles intact, not piercing [the soil] with a goad, but repeatedly encouraging [the oxen] by shouting. By this procedure he performs six furrows; thus it is called *ṣaṇṇivartanī*.

Regarding "the Kauddālī": near water, one digs with a spade, or a ploughshare, or a sharp piece of wood; one sows seeds and produces bulbs, roots, fruits, vegetables, and medicinal herbs. Because one works with a spade (*kuddāla*), it is called *Kauddālī*.
Then, having gone outside and muttered the *vyāhṛtis*, he mutters the consecration of the quarters:
"May Earth, the intermediate space, the sky, the stars, and the quarters;
may Agni, Vāyu, and Sūrya—may these deities protect me on the path. (8)

Having recited the *Mānastokīya* hymn and entered the village, he presents himself at every door along with his pack-load; because he is seen thus, they call him "Saṃdarśin" (the One Who Is Seen). Because he maintains his livelihood by that very [means] whenever there is no other means of subsistence, and because he lives steadfastly by that alone, he is celebrated as "Dhruva" (the Steadfast).

"Saṃprakṣālanī" means the discarding of herbs that have grown; there is no placing [aside] or accumulation. It is called "saṃprakṣālanī" because one washes the vessels thoroughly and turns them upside down. ||11||

"Samūhā": In places where there is no prohibition—whether on paths, in fields, or in open spaces—wherever medicinal herbs are found, one gathers them by means of gathering (samūhanī) and subsists upon them; thus it is called "gathering" (samūhā). 12.
"Pālanī" means non-violence; this is what is expressed here. It is called "pālanī" because it desires husked grains from virtuous people, or because it protects the seeds. 13.

"Śiloñcha" means: in places where there is no prohibition—whether on paths, in fields, or in open spaces wherever herbs are found—one gathers a single ear of grain from each place and subsists from time to time on those gleanings; thus it is called "gleaning" (śiloñcha). ||14||

Regarding *kāpotī*: in unobstructed places, on paths, in fields, or in any open space where medicinal herbs are found, one gathers each herb individually with the fingers by pinching it between the thumb and forefinger; because this is done like a pigeon (*kapota*), it is called *kāpotī*. 15.

"Siddhecchā" means: one who is exhausted by his activities, or due to old age or the depletion of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*), desires cooked food from virtuous people; thus he is called *siddhecchā*. For him, there exists the attribution [of the status] to himself, a formal designation like that of a renunciant (*saṃnyāsin*), with the exception of the sacred grass ring (*pavitraka*) and the saffron-colored garment (*kāṣāyavāsa*).

Or else, "forest-dweller" (*vānyā*) refers to those who subsist on wild trees, creepers, climbing plants, medicinal herbs, and grasses such as *śyāmāka* and *jartila*. Thus, one who subsists by means of forest products is a *vānyā*. Furthermore, they cite this: "Moving about with deer, dwelling together with them, and a mode of life similar to theirs—this is the visible mark of heaven."
The definition of heaven is perception. ||19||
Thus ends the second chapter of the third book in the Dharma-sūtra of Baudhāyana.
Now, there are two kinds of forest-dwellers (vānaprastha): [those who] cook and those who do not cook.

In that regard, there are five kinds of *pacamānaka* practitioners: those who live entirely in the forest (*sarvāraṇyaka*), those who remove the husks from grain (*vaituṣika*), those who subsist on bulbs and roots (*kandamūlabhakṣa*), those who subsist on fruits (*phalabhakṣa*), and those who subsist on vegetables (*śākabhakṣa*). ||3||

In that regard, those known as "all-forest-dwellers" (sarvāraṇyaka) resort to two kinds of forest life: those who subsist on what has been infused by Indra (indrāvasikta) and those who subsist on what has been infused with semen (reto’vasikta). Among them, those called "infused by Indra" bring back creepers, shrubs, climbing plants, and trees; having cooked them and offered the Agnihotra oblation both morning and evening, and having given portions to ascetics, guests, and those observing vows, they eat the remainder. Those called "infused with semen" bring back meat killed by tigers, wolves, hawks, or any other such predator; having cooked it and offered the Agnihotra oblation both morning and evening, and having given portions to ascetics and guests, they eat the remainder.

The Vaituṣikas, however, having brought rice grains excluding husked grain and having cooked them, perform the Agnihotra sacrifice morning and evening, give [the food] to ascetics, guests, and those observing vows, and then eat the remainder as their portion.
The same applies even to those who subsist on bulbs, roots, fruits, and vegetables. ||8||

There are exactly five types of those who diminish their intake: those who emerge [from water] once a day, those who eat what comes [to them], those who take food with the mouth, those who subsist on water, and those who subsist on air. ||9||

Among them, those called *unmajjakas* exclude the use of iron and stone implements. (10) Those who eat by taking [food] with their hands (*hastapravṛttāśins*) take it with their hands. (11) Those who take [food] with their mouths (*mukhādadinas*) take it with their mouths. (12) Those whose food is water (*toyāhāras*) subsist on water alone. (13) There are also those who subsist on air (*vāyubhakṣas*) and those who are without food (*nirāhāras*). (14)

Thus, ten initiations (dīkṣās) are prescribed for the Vaikhānasas. (15) He who, having undertaken his own scripture, [observes] the staff, silence, and vigilance; (16) the Vaikhānasas are purified when they are without food—thus it is said. (17) The acceptance of the scripture is mandatory for all Brahman-Vaikhānasas. (18)
One should not harm gadflies or mosquitoes; such a person becomes a Himavat ascetic, established in the forest, contented, and fond of rags, skins, and water.
A forest-dweller, devoted to austerity, should first honor guests who arrive at his hermitage at the proper time, as well as the gods, the brahmins, and the sacred fire.
On that day, he adopted a difficult, unassailable, and common mode of life shared with beasts and birds,
subsisting on a diet of astringent and bitter foods gathered from the people.
Having embraced this auspicious way of life, which is shunned by the wicked,
and having taken refuge in dwelling in the forest, a Brahmin does not come to grief.
Moving about together with the deer, dwelling with them alone,
and having a way of life identical to theirs— this is the visible mark of heaven.
The definition of heaven is direct perception. ||22||
Thus ends the third chapter of the third book in the Dharma-sūtra of Baudhāyana.

Now, if a religious student (*brahmacārin*), while acting as if contrary to his vow, should eat meat or have sexual intercourse with a woman—even in times of all kinds of distress—[he shall perform the following]: having kindled a fire in the inner chamber and strewn grass around it, and having performed the rites beginning with the oblation to Agni, he then offers additional oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*):
"By desire was it done; desire does it; for desire alone is all this. To him who causes me to do it, *svāhā*!
By mind was it done; mind does it; for mind alone is all this. To him who causes me to do it, *svāhā*!"
That which was created by *rajas* creates *rajas*; all this belongs to *rajas* alone—to him who makes me do it, *svāhā*!
That which was created by *tamas* creates *tamas*; all this belongs to *tamas* alone—to him who makes me do it, *svāhā*!
That which was created by evil (*pāpman*) creates evil; all this belongs to evil alone—to him who makes me do it, *svāhā*!
What was done by wrath, wrath does; indeed, all this is just wrath. "To him who makes me do it, svāhā! ||2||

The rite is completed beginning with the *jaya* formulas up until the gift of the cow as a boon. To the west of the fire, he remains covered by a black antelope skin with its neck pointing eastward and the hair side up.

When dawn has broken, having drawn himself away from the rear part [of the sacrificial ground], gone to a sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*), and bathed according to the established rule, he remains submerged in the water and performs sixteen breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) with the *aghamaṛṣaṇa* hymn; then, having performed the established worship of the Sun (*ādityopasthāna*), he goes to the house of his teacher. 5.
One should understand this to be exactly like the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) of the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha). ||6||
Thus ends the fourth chapter of the third book in the Dharma-sūtra of Baudhāyana.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the ritual procedure for the Aghamarṣaṇa, which is the most purifying of purifiers. 1.

Having gone to a sacred bathing place (tīrtha) and bathed, wearing clean clothes, he should clear a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) at the water’s edge and, with a garment moistened once and with his hand moistened once, recite the Aghamarṣaṇa as a private study while facing the sun. (2) He should do so one hundred times in the morning, one hundred times at midday, and one hundred times in the afternoon, or an unlimited number of times. (3) When the stars have risen, he should consume a handful of barley-gruel. (4)

One is released from minor offenses (*upapātaka*) committed intentionally or unintentionally after seven nights, provided one excludes the killing of an embryo, violating the teacher’s bed, stealing gold, and drinking liquor; [these may be removed] after twelve nights. After twenty-one nights, one overcomes even those [grave sins] and conquers them as well.

"He crosses over everything, he conquers everything, he obtains the fruit of all sacrifices; he becomes as one who has bathed in all sacred fords, one who has fulfilled his vows in all the Vedas, and one known by all the gods. He purifies the line of sight and his ritual acts are accomplished," so says Baudhāyana. ||7||
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the third book of the Baudhāyana Dharmasūtra.

Now, if one should regard oneself as heavy with the weight of one's own performed actions, one should cook a handful of barley-gruel for one's own sake when the stars have risen. (1) One should not offer it into the fire. (2) Nor is there an offering of bali-oblations here. (3) One should consecrate the uncooked, the cooking, and the cooked [gruel] with mantras. (4)
You are barley; you are the king of grains; you belong to Varuṇa and are joined with honey.
You are the cleanser of all evils, remembered as a purifier by the seers.
Barley is ghee, barley is honey, and barley is indeed the nectar of immortality;
may they purify all my evil, whatever misdeed has been committed by me.
Whatever deed has been done by speech, whatever deed has been done by action, and whatever has been ill-conceived by the mind—
may the barley grains purify all that misfortune and Kālakarṇī for me.
May the barley grains purify for me all that has been defiled by a dog or a pig, that which has been touched by the remnants of a crow's meal, and my failure to serve my mother and father.
O barley grains, purify for me everything— terrible royal offenses joined with great sins, as well as the unrighteousness of children and the aged.
The theft of gold, the violation of vows, officiating at the sacrifice of one for whom it is forbidden,
and reviling Brahmins— may all these be purified for me by the barley grains.

May all these foods purify me: the food of a group, the food of a courtesan, the food of a Śūdra, food from a funeral rite or a period of impurity, the food of a thief, and the food from a recent funeral—may all these be purified by barley.

While [the oblation] is being cooked, one should perform protection with the following: "Homage to Rudra, the lord of beings! The sky is peaceful! and with this *anuvāka*, "Make your strength like a wide-extending net," and with the five sections beginning, "The gods who dwell in the east, led by Agni, slayers of demons," and with the two verses, "May there be no harm to our offspring" and "The Brahman among the gods. 6.
And being self-restrained, he should eat what is cooked and light, having poured it into a vessel.

"Those gods who are born of the mind, yoked by the mind, highly skillful, with Dakṣa as their father—may they protect us, may they favor us; homage to them, svāhā to them!"—thus one should offer into oneself. ||8||

One who desires intelligence [should drink it] for three nights. (9) Having drunk it for six nights, an evildoer becomes pure. (10) Having drunk it for seven nights, one purifies even the killing of a learned Brahmin (*bhrūṇahatyā*), violating the Guru’s bed, stealing gold, and drinking liquor. (11) Having drunk it for eleven nights, one casts off even the sins committed by one's ancestors. (12)

"Or else, having drunk barley-grains that have emerged from a cow for twenty-one nights, one sees the hosts, one sees the lord of the hosts, one sees the lore, and one sees the lord of the lore; thus said the Blessed Baudhāyana. (13)
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the third book of the Dharma-sūtra of Baudhāyana.

One who considers himself impure should offer oblations with the *kūśmāṇḍa* formulas. "As is a thief, as is a killer of an embryo, so becomes he who sheds seed in a place that is not the womb. From whatever sin short of the killing of an embryo he has committed, from that he is released. (1–3)

Having discharged semen in a non-vaginal place, except during sleep, one who is free from taint and desires purification [should perform this]. (4) On either the new moon day or the full moon day, having had his hair, beard, body hair, and nails shaved, he undertakes the vow according to the rule for a student (*brahmacārin*). (5) This lasts for a year, a month, twenty-four days, twelve nights, six nights, or three nights. (6) He shall not eat meat, he shall not approach a woman, he shall not sit on elevated ground, and he shall loathe falsehood. (7)

Subsisting on milk is the first rule; or, consuming barley-gruel, he should perform the twelve-night *kṛcchra* penance or beg for alms. (8) In such cases, a Kṣatriya [should consume] rice-gruel, and a Vaiśya, curdled milk. (9)

In the forenoon, having kindled the fire according to the rules for the *pākayajña* sacrifices and having strewn grass around it, he performs the *agnimukha* rite and then offers oblations of clarified butter with these three sections: "Whatever offense against the gods," "Whatever debt I incurred while not gambling," and "Bestowing life upon you from all sides. (10) He should offer the clarified butter verse by verse. (11) He offers four spoonfuls with the verses beginning, "The lion, the tiger, and the viper... Having offered the four "returning" oblations with the verses, "O Agni, come back," "O Agni Aṅgiras," "With strength again," and "Together with wealth," he stands in the world of the sacrificer with fuel-sticks in hand and worships with the twelve-verse hymn beginning, "We announce [this] to Vaiśvānara. (12)

"Whatever sin has ever been committed by me through mind or speech—from all that, O Agni, deliver me; for you indeed know the truth as it is. Having said "Svāhā! and placed the fuel-stick upon the fire, he bestows a boon. ||13||
The rite is established as beginning with the Jaya-oblation and ending with the gift of the cow as a boon. There is only one attendant at the fire.

Now, regarding the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*): having offered the full-oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the verses, "Whatever offense against the gods," "Whatever debt I incurred while not gambling," and "Bestowing long life upon you from every side," he should proceed. Having offered with the *daśahotr* formula, one who is about to begin the *agnihotra*; having offered with the *caturhotr*, one who is about to begin the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices; having offered with the *pañcahotr*, one who is about to begin the *cāturmāsya* sacrifices; having offered with the *ṣaḍḍhotr*, at the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*); and having offered with the *saptahotr*, at the *soma* sacrifice.

And it is known: "With these [verses] one should offer oblations over the ritual acts and so forth; purified, he attains the worlds of the gods"—for such is the Brāhmaṇa. For such is the Brāhmaṇa. 18.
Thus ends the seventh chapter of the third book in the Dharma-sūtra of Baudhāyana.

Now, therefore, we shall explain the ritual procedure for the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. (1) One should fast on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight. (2) Having had his hair, beard, body hair, and nails shaved—or at least his beard—wearing unwashed clothes and speaking the truth, he should enter his dwelling. (3)

In that [fire], his fire—either once-kindled or produced by churning from two fire-sticks—is established. A student or a friend should be prepared to deliver the instructions. And there should be sacrificial food fit for the commencement of the vow.

Having kindled the fire and strewn grass around it, and having performed the rites beginning with the oblation to Agni, he offers portions of the cooked food. (7) He offers to Agni; to whichever lunar day it may be; to the lunar mansion together with its presiding deity; here he offers with the verse, "At this [sacrifice] the cow has assented"; to the lunar deity on the fifth; to Heaven and Earth on the sixth; to Day and Night on the seventh; to Rudra on the eighth; to Sūrya on the ninth; to Varuṇa on the tenth; to Indra on the eleventh; and to the Viśvedevas on the twelfth. (8) Furthermore, others prescribe offerings to the quarters together with their presiding deities, and to the broad intermediate space together with its presiding deity. (9)

Having offered the oblation to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt with the verse, "Being born, he becomes ever new," he then draws out this remnant of the sacrificial food into a bronze vessel or a wooden cup, pours over it condiments made from sacrificial grains, and eats fifteen morsels in their natural order. He eats the first with the words, "For out-breathing (prāṇa) thee! the second with "For down-breathing (apāna) thee! the third with "For through-breathing (vyāna) thee! the fourth with "For up-breathing (udāna) thee! and the fifth with "For equal-breathing (samāna) thee! When there are four [morsels], he eats the first two together; when there are three, he eats the first two together; when there are two, he eats the first one together with three; and the last one with all [the remaining formulas].
"O Nigrābhya waters!
Having drunk the water, he then offers oblations of clarified butter:
"May my prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, and samāna be purified; may I become light, free from passion, and free from evil—svāhā!"
Speech and mind: oṃ.
Head and hands: oṃ.
Skin, hide, and flesh: oṃ.

"Oṃ! May sound, touch, and form [be purified]. Oṃ! Earth, water, and fire [be purified]. May my self consisting of food, the self consisting of vital breath, the self consisting of mind, the self consisting of consciousness, and the self consisting of bliss be purified for me.
