May I become light, stainless, and free from evil, svāhā!"—[with these words] he recites the seven sections (anuvākas). ||12||

The rite is accomplished beginning with the Jaya-hymns and ending with the gift of the cow. (13) He worships the Sun with verses addressed to Sūrya and the Moon with verses addressed to Candra. (14) As he is about to lie down, he mutters the verse: "O Agni, do thou keep watch well. (15) Upon waking, he mutters: "O Agni, you are the guardian of vows. (16)

One should not converse with women or Śūdras, nor should one look at urine or excrement. (17) Having seen something impure, one mutters: "The mind is unbound, the eye is poor; Sūrya is the best of lights; O consecration, do not abandon me! (18)

On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, he takes fourteen mouthfuls. (19) In this manner, by decreasing one [mouthful] each day, he continues until the new moon. (20) On the new moon day, no mouthful is taken. (21) Then, on the first day of the bright fortnight, he takes one; on the second, two. (22) In this manner, by increasing one [mouthful] each day, he continues until the full moon. (23) On the full moon day, he offers the *sthālīpāka* sacrifice to Agni, to whichever lunar day (*tithi*) it may fall, and to the constellations (*nakṣatra*) together with their presiding deities. (24) Having offered the sacrifice to Abhijit together with its deity prior to Śroṇā, he should give a cow to the Brahmins. (25)

This *cāndrāyaṇa* is the "ant-middled" (*pipīlikāmadhya*); when performed in reverse, it is the "barley-middled" (*yavamadhya*). (26) Having performed either of these, a doer of evil becomes purified from all mortal sins (*pātaka*). (27) They say that this is to be undertaken for each specific desire. (28) Whatever desire one may have, one attains it by means of this. (29) By means of this, the seers (*ṛṣi*) purified themselves and accomplished their past deeds. This [rite] is auspicious, meritorious, beneficial for sons, beneficial for grandsons, beneficial for cattle, conducive to long life, leading to heaven, conducive to fame, and fulfilling all desires. (30) He who studies this attains the splendor of the stars and union with, and residence in the same world as, the sun and the moon; he who studies this attains [these]. (31)
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the third book of the Baudhāyana Dharmasūtra.

Now, therefore, we shall explain the rule for the *pārāyaṇa* performed while fasting. (1) He should wear clean garments or garments made of bark. (2) He should desire sacrificial food, water, or fruits. (3)

Having gone out from the village toward the eastern or northern direction, having smeared a square sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) the size of a cow-hide with cow-dung, having sprinkled it with water, having drawn the ritual lines (*lakṣaṇa*), and having sprinkled it again with water, he should kindle the fire, strew grass around it, and offer oblations to these deities: to Agni, svāhā; to Prajāpati, svāhā; to Soma, svāhā; to the Viśvedevas; to the Self-existent One; to the Ṛg-verses, Yajus-formulas, Sāman-chants, and Atharvan-hymns; to Faith, Understanding, Memory, Prosperity, Modesty, Savitṛ, Sāvitrī, the Lord of the Assembly (*Sadasaspati*), and Anumati. (4)

Having offered the oblation, he should begin with the beginning of the Vedas and study them continuously. (5) He should not speak in between, nor should he pause in between. (6) But if he should speak in between, or if he should pause in between, he should perform three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) and begin again from the point where he left off. (7) In the case of a lack of understanding, he should study that portion for as long as it takes until he knows it—whether by the *ṛc*, the *yajus*, or the *sāman*. (8) Then he should study its *brāhmaṇa*, its phonology (*chāndasa*), and its deities (*daivata*). (9)

One should study twelve collections of the Veda. Whatever one has studied during improper times for recitation, whatever has caused anger among the teachers, and whatever forbidden acts one has committed—one purifies oneself by means of these [recitations]. His sacred knowledge (*brahman*) becomes pure and purified. (10) From this point upward, there is accumulation. (11) Having studied another twelve collections of the Veda, by means of them one attains the world of Uśanas. (12) Having studied another twelve collections of the Veda, by means of them one attains the world of Bṛhaspati. (13) Having studied another twelve collections of the Veda, by means of them one attains the world of Prajāpati. (14) Without eating, one should study a thousand collections of the Veda. Having become the *brahman*, free from passion, he becomes the *brahman*. (15)

One who subsists on alms for a year attains divine vision. One who eats barley-gruel for six months, water-mash for four months, fruit for two months, water for one month, or fasts for twelve nights, quickly becomes invisible; he purifies his kinsmen—seven descendants and seven ancestors—and he purifies himself as the fifteenth, as well as the row [of eaters] at his meal.

This very thing they call the "support of the gods" (*devaniśrayaṇī*). By means of this, indeed, the gods attained godhood and the seers attained seerhood. Now, for this very sacrifice, there are indeed three times for its commencement: at the morning pressing, at the midday pressing, or in the Brahma-watch of the night. Prajāpati proclaimed this to the seven seers; the seven seers [proclaimed it] to Mahājajñu; Mahājajñu [proclaimed it] to the Brahmins—yes, to the Brahmins.
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the third book of the Dharma-sūtra of Baudhāyana.
The duty of the social classes and the duty of the stages of life have been explained. ||1||

Now, this person may act falsely through a blameworthy deed: either he officiates at a sacrifice for one for whom it is forbidden to officiate, or he accepts a gift from one from whom it is forbidden to accept, or he eats the food of one whose food is forbidden to eat, or he behaves in a manner that is not to be practiced. Regarding this, they deliberate: "Should one perform an expiation, or should one not?"

"For indeed, karma is not exhausted" [is the saying]. "One should simply act," [it is said]. It is known from scripture: "Having sacrificed with the Punastoma, they return to the Soma-pressing. Furthermore, they cite: "He who sacrifices with the Aśvamedha overcomes all evil; he overcomes even the murder of a Brahmin. And: "One who is being falsely accused should sacrifice with the Agniṣṭut."

The means of atonement for that [sin] are: recitation (*japa*), austerity (*tapas*), burnt offerings (*homa*), fasting (*upavāsa*), and giving (*dāna*). (9) The *Upaniṣads*, the beginning and end of the Vedas, the *Saṃhitās* of all the meters, the *Madhu* hymns, the *Aghamarṣaṇa*, the *Atharvaśiras*, the *Rudras*, the *Puruṣasūkta*, the *Rājana* and *Rauhiṇa* *Sāmans*, the *Bṛhat* and *Rathantara*, the *Puruṣagati*, the *Mahānāmnīs*, the *Mahāvairāja*, the *Mahādivākīrtya*, any one of the *Jyeṣṭhasāmans*, the *Bahiṣpavamāna*, the *Kūṣmāṇḍas*, the *Pāvamānīs*, and the *Sāvitrī*—these are the purifiers (*pāvana*). (10) Living on milk according to the rule of subsistence, eating vegetables, eating fruits, eating roots, the *prasṛti-yāvaka* fast, the consumption of gold, the consumption of clarified butter, and the drinking of *Soma*—these are the purifying practices (*medhya*). (11) All mountains, all flowing rivers, sacred lakes, holy bathing places (*tīrtha*), the dwellings of seers (*ṛṣi-niketana*), cow-pens, fields, and sacred groves (*pariṣkanda*)—these are the [purifying] places (*deśa*). (12) Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, touching water at the three daily libations (*savana*), service to the teacher, celibacy, sleeping on the ground, wearing a single garment, and fasting—these are the austerities (*tapas*). (13) Gold, a cow, clothing, a horse, land, sesame seeds, clarified butter, and food—these are the things to be given (*deya*). (14) One year, six months, four, three, two, or one month; twenty-four days, twelve days, six days, three days, a day and night, or a single day—these are the durations of time (*kāla*). (15)

These [penances] shall be performed when no specific instruction is given. (16) In cases of heavy sins, the penances are heavy; in cases of light sins, they are light. (17) The Kṛcchra, the Atikṛcchra, and the Cāndrāyaṇa constitute the universal expiation. This is the universal expiation. (18)
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the third book of the Baudhāyana Dharmasūtra.
Thus ends the third question.
We shall now describe the various expiations, each distinct for its purpose, which are either heavy or light according to their respective faults. (1)

For if something were appropriate here, he would have pointed it out right there; likewise, among the more serious [faults] he has mentioned them repeatedly, while for the minor ones he has mentioned only a few. (2)
One should perform breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) according to the procedure seen in the scriptures.
Whatever sin has been committed by the genitals, or whatever may have been done by the feet,
by the arms, by the mind, by speech, or by the ear, skin, nose, and eyes— [all that is purified].
Alternatively, in cases of transgressions involving the eyes, ears, skin, nose, or mind, one becomes pure through three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas). ||4||

In the case of eating the food of a Śūdra, sexual intercourse with a woman [of forbidden class], or eating [forbidden food] alone—each of these separately—one should perform seven breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) for seven days each. ||5|| In the case of consuming what is not to be eaten, what is not to be consumed, what is not to be drunk, or what is not to be tasted; likewise, in the sale of forbidden goods—with the exception of honey, meat, ghee, oil, alkaline substances, salt, and inferior food—and whatever else is of a similar nature, one should perform twelve breath-restraints for twelve days each. ||6|| In the case of those sins other than mortal transgressions (pātaka) and minor transgressions (upapātaka), and whatever else is of a similar nature, one should perform twelve breath-restraints for half a month each. ||7|| In the case of those sins other than mortal transgressions and major transgressions leading to loss of caste (patanīya), and whatever else is of a similar nature, one should perform twelve breath-restraints for twelve days each. ||8|| In the case of those sins other than mortal transgressions, and whatever else is of a similar nature, one should perform twelve breath-restraints for twelve half-months each. ||9|| Now, in the case of mortal transgressions, one should perform twelve breath-restraints for one year each. ||10||
One should give an unmarried girl to a virtuous man who observes celibacy;
or, even to one lacking in virtues, one should not withhold her once she has reached her menses.
He who does not give away a maiden in marriage after she has reached her menses for three years undoubtedly incurs a guilt equal to that of killing an embryo. ||12||
If he does not beg, it would be so; but if he begs, Manu has declared that there is a fault and a sin in each and every season.
A woman who has reached puberty should wait for her father’s command for three years;
thereafter, in the fourth year, she may take a suitable husband. If no suitable man is available, she may resort even to one lacking in good qualities. (14)

If a maiden has been abducted by force, provided she has not been consecrated with the sacred mantras, she should be given to another according to the prescribed rite; for she remains just as a maiden as before.
If, after she has been given away or even after the fire-oblation has been offered, her husband should die,
and she remains a virgin, having returned from his house,
she deserves to undergo the marriage rite again according to the law for remarried women (paunarbhava).
He who does not approach his wife when she is in her season for three years undoubtedly incurs a guilt equal to that of killing an embryo. ||17||
If a man does not approach his wife when she has bathed after her menses and is present before him, his ancestors lie within that menstrual flow for that entire month. (18)

They say that the fault of him who does not approach his wife during her season and of him who approaches her outside her season is equal, as is the fault of him who discharges seed in a place other than the womb. (19)
If a wife should violate her sacred duty by being unfaithful to her husband,
she shall be proclaimed as a destroyer of the embryo in the midst of the village and banished from the house.
If he does not approach his wife when she has bathed after her menses— she being self-restrained and devoted to dharma—
it is prescribed that for such transgression of his vow, he must perform one hundred breath-control exercises (prāṇāyāmas).
Seated with the sacred thread in hand, one should practice the daily Vedic study (brahma), as well as breath control (prāṇāyāma), purificatory formulas (pavitra), the Vyāhṛtis, and the Praṇava. 22.
Always disciplined, he should repeatedly perform breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma);
from the tips of his hair to the ends of his nails, he performs the highest austerity. 23.
From cessation wind is born; from wind fire is born;
from heat water is produced; thus it is purified internally by these three. ||24||
Knowledge is attained through yoga; yoga is the defining characteristic of dharma.
All virtues have their root in yoga; therefore, one should always be disciplined in yoga. ||25||
The three Vedas, beginning with the syllable Om, are established within the Praṇava;
the Praṇava and the Vyāhṛtis are indeed the eternal, primeval Brahman.
For one who is constantly disciplined in the *praṇava*, in the seven *vyāhṛtis*, and in the three-footed *gāyatrī*, no fear exists anywhere. (27)
One should recite the Gāyatrī, together with the Vyāhṛtis, the Praṇava, and the Śiras, three times while restraining the breath; that is called prāṇāyāma. (28)
Sixteen breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), accompanied by the vyāhṛtis and the praṇava, when practiced day after day, purify even the killer of a learned Brahmin within a month. (29)
This is the foremost austerity, this is the defining characteristic of dharma;
for the purpose of destroying all defects, this alone is distinguished as supreme.
This very [point] is further specified: ||30||
Thus ends the first chapter of the fourth book in the Dharma-sūtra of Baudhāyana.

For whatever is appropriate in a particular case, that indeed should be taught therein; repeatedly, in matters of greater weight, one should likewise apply the lesser [remedies], and in minor matters, the smallest. //2//
One should prescribe the penances according to the procedure seen in the scriptures. ||3||
But one who is about to receive [a gift], or having already received it, should likewise recite the four *ṛc* verses beginning with "taratsamandī. (4)

But for all those whose food is unfit to be eaten, if one eats the food of such a person, purification from the sin is achieved by performing the *mārjana* rite with the *taratsamandī* verses of the Rigveda. (5)
The procedure for the expiation of foeticide is another; I shall explain that hereafter, by which procedure one is liberated from all sins whatsoever.
For twelve nights, he should perform breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*), recite the purificatory *vyāhṛtis* as well as the *praṇava*, and mutter the *aghamarṣaṇa* hymn while subsisting on milk.
Or, for three nights, subsisting on air alone, wearing wet clothes, or having bathed, he becomes pure.
"Even after repeatedly practicing prohibited conducts, one is liberated from all sins by performing the Vāruṇī offerings. (9)

Then, on the night of the new moon, an *avakīrṇin* (one who has broken his vow of celibacy) shall kindle the fire and, having performed the ritual attendances required for a *dārvī-homa*, he offers two oblations of clarified butter: "Desire, I have been sprinkled; I have been sprinkled, O Desire! To Desire, svāhā! Desire, I have been deceived; I have been deceived, O Desire! To Desire, svāhā! Having offered these, with hands joined in reverence, he shall worship the fire from a slightly oblique direction, saying:
"May the Maruts sprinkle me, may Indra sprinkle me, may Bṛhaspati sprinkle me;
may this Agni sprinkle me with long life and with strength—make me long-lived!"

The Maruts restore his vital breaths; Indra restores his strength; Bṛhaspati restores his spiritual luster; Agni restores everything else. Having become whole in body, he attains a full lifespan. He should consecrate [the food] three times; for it is known that "the gods are indeed threefold in truth. (11)
He who might consider himself as if unpurified by minor offenses (upapātaka) is liberated from all evil by performing this oblation according to the prescribed rule. ||12||

Alternatively, having intentionally or unintentionally committed an act involving forbidden food, drink, or prohibited meals, or having emitted semen into a Śūdra woman or into a non-vaginal opening, one becomes pure by sipping water while reciting the *ābliṅga* and *vāruṇī* verses. Furthermore, they cite this:
"In the case of eating what should not be eaten, drinking what should not be drunk, consuming what is prohibited, or performing an action contrary to dharma..."
Moreover, even when the intellect is active, one is purified from sins equal to the great crimes, and indeed from all transgressions. ||14||

Or, fasting for three nights and entering the water three times a day, restraining his vital breaths within himself, he should recite the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times; Manu has declared that this is equal to the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) of a horse sacrifice. ||15||
And it is known:
"The foot is a wide-spread, ancient purifier, by which one who is purified crosses over evil deeds."
"Purified by that pure and holy [soma], may we cross over evil and hostility. ||16||

We shall now declare the penances that have not been specifically mentioned; how they should apply in cases of negligence for those who are composed and disciplined. (1)

With all the *vyāhṛtis* preceded by *oṃ*, one should sip water for purification from all sins. (2) That which he sips first, with that he gratifies the *Ṛgveda*; that which he sips second, with that the *Yajurveda*; that which he sips third, with that the *Sāmaveda*. (3) That which he wipes [his lips] first, with that he gratifies the *Atharvaveda*; that which he wipes second, with that the *Itihāsa-Purāṇa*. (4) When he sprinkles his left hand, his feet, head, heart, nose, eyes, ears, and navel, with that he gratifies the plants, the trees, and all the deities. Therefore, through this very act of sipping water, one is liberated from every sin. (5)

Or he should offer eight fuel-sticks: "Thou art the expiation for the sin committed against the gods, svāhā! Thou art the expiation for the sin committed against men, svāhā! Thou art the expiation for the sin committed against the ancestors, svāhā! Thou art the expiation for the sin committed against oneself, svāhā! For whatever sin we have committed by day and by night, thou art its expiation, svāhā! For whatever sin we have committed while sleeping and while waking, thou art its expiation, svāhā! For whatever sin we have committed whether knowing or unknowing, thou art its expiation, svāhā! Thou art the expiation for every sin, svāhā! ||6||

Having offered these eight oblations, one is liberated from all evil. Furthermore, they cite this: the Aghamarṣaṇa, the Devakṛta, the Śuddhavatīs, the Taratsamās, the Kūṣmāṇḍyas, the Pāvamānyas, the Virajas, and the Mṛtyulāṅgala.
The Durgā verses, the Vyāhṛtis, and the Rudras are destroyers of great defects;
they are destroyers of great defects. ||8||
Thus ends the third chapter in the fourth book of the Baudhāyana Dharmasūtra.

"Ṛtaṃ ca satyaṃ ca"—by reciting this *aghamaṛṣaṇa* verse three times while submerged in water, one is liberated from all sin. (2) "Āyaṃ gauḥ pṛśnir akramīt"—by reciting this *ṛc* three times while submerged in water, one is liberated from all sin. (3) "Drupadād iva mumucānaḥ"—by reciting this *ṛc* three times while submerged in water, one is liberated from all sin. (4) "Haṃsaḥ śuciṣat"—by reciting this *ṛc* three times while submerged in water, one is liberated from all sin. (5) Or else, by reciting the *Sāvitrī* verse three times while submerged in water—first foot by foot, then half-verse by half-verse, and finally the whole verse—one is liberated from all sin. (6) Or else, by reciting the *vyāhṛtis* both individually and collectively three times while submerged in water, one is liberated from all sin. (7) Or else, by reciting the *praṇava* alone three times while submerged in water, one is liberated from all sin. (8)

This treatise on Dharma should not be given to one who is not a son, nor to one who is not a disciple, nor to one who has not lived with him for a year. A thousand [cows] with a bull as the eleventh is the sacrificial fee, or it may be the favor of the teacher; or it may be the favor of the teacher.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the fourth book of the Dharmasūtra of Baudhāyana.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the rites of the Sāman, Ṛg, Yajus, and Atharvan [Vedas], by which one quickly attains the desires held in the mind. (1)
Having purified one's own body through recitation, fire-offerings, oblations, yantras, and so forth, one should accomplish all rites; otherwise, one does not attain success.

A twice-born man, intending to perform recitations, fire-offerings, sacrifices, or mechanical rituals, should first have his hair and beard shaved on days that are bright, auspicious, and under favorable lunar mansions.
He should bathe at the three daily sessions, protect himself from anger and falsehood,
refrain from conversing with women or Śūdras, remain celibate, and observe the vow of the sacrificial oblation.
While sleeping during the day, one should pay homage to cows, Brahmins, ancestors, and gods;
likewise, while engaged in recitation, burnt offerings, sacrifices, or mechanical rituals, one should remain standing by day and seated at night.
The Prājāpatya penance consists of eating only what is unasked for during the day and at night,
followed by subsisting on air for twelve days, three days at a time.
One day and likewise one night, subsisting on air while remaining unrecognized—this threefold cycle repeated is called the *bāla-kṛcchra* (the child's penance). ||7||
One should eat each morsel for three days each according to the previously mentioned method;
for another three days, one should subsist on air alone—this is called the *atikṛcchra*. (8)
Subsisting on water for these three days, and thereafter subsisting on air, this third [penance] is to be known as the Kṛcchrātikṛcchra; it is exceedingly purifying.
For three days at a time, one should drink hot milk, clarified butter, and water boiled with *kuśa* grass;
for another three days, one should subsist on air alone—this is called the *taptakṛcchra*.
Cow’s urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water boiled with *kuśa* grass, followed by a fast for one night, is known as the *sāṃtapana-kṛcchra*. ||11||

Taking cow’s urine with the *gāyatrī* mantra, cow dung with "gandhadvārām," milk with "āpyāyasva," curd with "dadhikrāvṇo," clarified butter with "śukram asi jyotiḥ," and kuśa-water with "devasya tvā. (12)
One part of cow’s urine, half as much of dung, three parts of milk,
two of curd, one of ghee, and one of water infused with *kuśa* grass—
this is the *sāṃtapana* penance, which purifies even a dog-eater. 13.
Cow’s urine, cow dung, milk, curd, and likewise ghee—
one whose food for five nights consists of these five products of the cow is purified by the *pañcagavya*.
For one who is self-restrained and vigilant, fasting for twelve days is this penance called Parāka, which destroys all sins. ||15||
Those who expound the Veda declare that practicing each of these [penances] with cow urine and the other substances for twenty-one days constitutes the Mahāsāṃtapana Kṛcchra.
Increasing the morsels by one during the bright fortnight and decreasing them by one during the dark fortnight,
with two fast days at the end of the two fortnights— that indeed is known as the Cāndrāyaṇa.
A composed Brahmin should eat four morsels in the morning and four when the sun has set; thus he should perform the Śiśu-cāndrāyaṇa penance. 18.
With self-restraint, one should perform the *yaticāndrāyaṇa* penance by eating eight morsels of sacrificial food at midday for each month. (19)
By eating, for one month, eighty-two morsels of sacrificial food (haviṣya) in any manner whatsoever, O twice-born one, he attains the same world as the Moon.
Just as the rising moon dispels the world's fear of darkness,
so too does the twice-born man who performs the Cāndrāyaṇa penance destroy the fear of sin.
Subsisting on grain-particles, oil-cakes, buttermilk, barley-water, or air, for one, three, five, or seven days respectively— this Tulāpuruṣa rite destroys all sins.
Barley gruel for seven nights destroys the sins of embodied beings, or fasting for seven nights does so; this has been observed by the wise. (23)
In the months of Pauṣa, Bhādrapada, and Jyeṣṭha, by resorting to the Ārdrā constellation, the sky, and the sun respectively,
a twice-born man is freed from the three white sins, with the exception of those involving a fall from caste.
Cow’s urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water infused with *kuśa* grass,
combined with barley and *ācamana* water, constitute the extremely purifying *brahmakūrca*.
By fasting on the new moon day and eating only sesame seeds on the full moon day,
one is liberated from the sins committed during the bright and dark fortnights throughout the year by means of these sacred festivals.

One who subsists on almsfood is purified in one month from [the food of] those who maintain the sacred fires; from that of those who follow the Yāyāvara mode of life or dwell in the forest, one is purified in ten or five days. (27)
One who possesses wealth for a single day is purified by one day's fast;
one who subsists on the "pigeon-livelihood" (gleaning) is purified after drinking water for three days.
By reciting the *Ṛgveda*, *Yajurveda*, *Sāmaveda*, or any other Veda three times while fasting, one becomes supremely purifying. (29)
If, however, the one who subsists on air desires to perform it quickly, he should remain standing in water during the day; when he has emerged at dawn, that is equal to the Prājāpatya penance.
Having performed the recitation of the Gāyatrī eight thousand times when the sun has risen,
one is liberated from all sins, provided that one is not a killer of an embryo.
He who gives food, speaks the truth, and abides in compassion toward all beings surpasses all those previously mentioned who have been purified by the yantras. ||32||
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the fourth book of the Baudhāyana Dharmasūtra.
The Rudra-mantras with the *samādhucchandasa* verses, the *gāyatrī* accompanied by the *praṇava*, and the seven *vyāhṛtis* should be recited as they destroy all sins. (1)
The Mṛgāreṣṭi, the Pavitreṣṭi, the Trihavis, and the Pāvamānī sacrifices—these, when combined with the Vaiśvānarī, are destroyers of sin. ||2||
And understand this other secret which is being told:
one is liberated from all sins, except for the most grievous transgressions. (3)
Performing the purification with sacred blades of grass, reciting the Rudraikādaśinī, offering the sacred blades into the fire with clarified butter, and bestowing gold, cows, and sesame seeds; ||4||
He who should eat cooked barley-gruel mixed with cow urine, the essence of dung, along with curd, milk, and ghee, is liberated from sin in an instant. ||5||
He who has fathered a child upon a Śūdra woman, and he by whom an unapproachable woman has been violated—
both of them are liberated from that sin after seven nights by means of this rite.

In the case of consuming semen, urine, or feces; eating what is unfit to be eaten; performing the *paryādhāna* rite for one who has already had his fire kindled; performing a sacrifice for such a person; and for one who has neglected the sacred fires (*parivitti*), this [following penance] is the remedy.
"Even after committing very many acts that are not [necessarily] sins, one is liberated from all evils"—this is the teaching of the virtuous. (8)
The procedure for the authoritative means of the mantra path has been proclaimed, by which Bharadvāja and others attained identity with Brahman. (9)
With a serene heart, the brahmin, through the performance of this rite,
attains whatever various desires reside in his heart— whatever desires reside in his heart. (10)
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the fourth book of the Baudhāyana Dharmasūtra.
For that brahmin who has desisted from evil deeds and is engaged in meritorious deeds, his ritual actions succeed even without the use of yantras. ||1||
Therefore, those brahmins who are upright and purified by their straight actions quickly attain whatever they desire in their hearts. ||2||
Thus, these yogic exercises should be performed by the wise man for as long as it takes for the body to attain purity of the self. (3)
Then, having purified himself by means of these diagrams and having fasted for three nights,
he should begin that rite through which he desires to attain supernatural power (*ṛddhi*).
The *kṣmāpavitra*, the *sahasrākṣa*, the *mṛgāra*, the two *aṃhomuc* hymns, the *pāvamānī* verses, the *kūśmāṇḍya* verses, and those verses addressed to Vaiśvānara—[these are the purifiers]. (5)
Offering oblations of rice cooked with ghee three times a day for seven days, observing a vow of silence, eating sacrificial food, and restraining the activities of his senses; ||6||
If one gazes upon a lion reflected in a vessel filled with water at a crossroads, saying "ma" (me),
one is released from all sins, even from a great heinous crime.
Whatever accumulation of evil was committed in old age, youth, or childhood, and even that which was done in previous births out of ignorance—from all that one is liberated. (8)
Having fed the twice-born with milk-rice mixed with ghee at the conclusion, and having bestowed cows, land, sesame seeds, and gold upon those who have eaten; 9.
The Brahmin becomes purified in soul, with the fuel of his sins completely consumed;
he thus becomes fit for rites performed for specific desires as well as for rites such as the establishment of the sacred fires.
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the fourth book of the *Dharmasūtra* of Baudhāyana.
He who performs this rite out of excessive greed or through negligence becomes possessed by the sin of another and perishes like one who has swallowed poison. ||1||
Performing this rite for his teacher, his father, his mother, and himself, the Brahmin shines like the sun; therefore, this rite is to be performed for them.
Who, by means of this thousand-eyed purifier, made Agni, Vāyu, Ravi, Soma, Yama, and the other lords of the gods pure? (3)
Whatever merit is renowned here in the three worlds, beginning with that of the Brahmins—by whom was that performed through this purifying rite? (4)
This secret [teaching] concerning Prajāpati is the first to arise and destroys sin;
after it, thousands of purifying [texts] have subsequently emerged. (5)
He who offers these eight groups [of oblations] for the years, solstices, seasons,
fortnights, and days, purifies ten ancestors and ten descendants of his own lineage.
Even while remaining on earth, he is recognized by the immortals dwelling in heaven as one of meritorious deeds;
furthermore, the doer of merit rejoices like a god even in the heavenly world. (7)
If a twice-born man is unable to offer these eight groups, even a single one must be offered by him; by that, his impurity is destroyed.
He whose sons or disciples offer these eight groups [of mantras] is also liberated from sin by means of those [offerings] purchased through teaching. //9//
Even by means of those purchased with wealth, one who desires to destroy his own sin must perform oblations;
for when he is incapable, he should not cause the bearer of the body to despair.
The renunciation of wealth is performed, as well as that of even well-performed deeds; sometimes the liberation of a man from sin, once he is free from debt, is accomplished. (11)
Liberated from the ocean of all debts of sin by this method,
he considers himself pure and capable of accomplishing his task.
But whatever actions a person whose soul is liberated from the debt of all sins undertakes, they attain perfection without effort, being one of purified body. (13)
This meritorious [text] concerning Prajāpati was proclaimed by the seer.
One who constantly teaches this, retains it in memory, or even hears it, is liberated from all sins and is glorified in the world of Brahmā. ||14||
One who desires to accomplish those mantras should mutter them for twelve days, having eaten rice once at night with ghee, milk, and curd. 15.
Likewise, the oblation with clarified butter should be performed ten times during each of the three daily pressings;
this constitutes the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*) for these mantras in the accomplishment of rites.
Thus it is said: "for the accomplishment of rites through the mantras. (16)
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the fourth book of the Baudhāyana Dharmasūtra.
